title: Buffalo Bills to address seating sightline concerns on a case-by-case basis at new $2.1B stadium
description: The Buffalo Bills are responding to criticism over various issues at their new stadium — including partially obstructed sightline concerns -- by addressing them on a case-by-case basis, the team announced Monday.  One of the larger concerns were seats with obstructed views, with several photos emerging on social media.  The seats were in the last row of the Section 417 of the northwest corner of the stadium, and the view of the far end zone was mostly blocked by the outcropping of the press box.
fullText:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. (AP) — The Buffalo Bills are responding to criticism over various issues at their new stadium — including partially obstructed sightline concerns -- by addressing them on a case-by-case basis, the team announced Monday.

The criticism stems from fans getting their first full experience inside the $2.1 billion Highmark Stadium during the Bills annual Blue and Red practice on Saturday night. Though the Bills said a majority of the feedback was overwhelmingly positive, a few complaints arose, which team president Pete Guelli termed as coming from less than 1% of the personal seat licensing holders.

One of the larger concerns were seats with obstructed views, with several photos emerging on social media.

The team said at least one photo taken by The Associated Press was from seats that were not placed on sale for football games. The seats were in the last row of the Section 417 of the northwest corner of the stadium, and the view of the far end zone was mostly blocked by the outcropping of the press box.

A team official said those seats could be used for other events taking place in the stadium, such as concerts, where the view would not be obstructed.

Other photos showed seats where views were partially obstructed by railings and staircases.

In selling the seats, prospective ticket buyers were given a virtual tour of the stadium that included visuals what their view of the field would resemble.

The team said it will review each complaint and use "the next six weeks to refine any details," in leading up to the Bills regular-season home-opener against Detroit on Sept. 17.

Next up for the Bills are two home preseason games, starting with the team hosting Carolina on Saturday.

The stadium's design was influenced by that of soccer's Premier League Tottenham Hotspur's home, which also hosts NFL games in London.

Bills owner Terry Pegula was impressed by noting that there are very few bad seats in the Hotspur stadium. The same, the Bills said, would apply to Highmark Stadium, which has a seating capacity of 60,108.

title: 76ers star LeBron James catches a stray from Hilary Duff
description: Hilary Duff teased LeBron James over his frequent team-jumping at a Philadelphia concert, following James' recent move to the 76ers.
fullText:
The world is still getting used to LeBron James being on the Philadelphia 76ers' roster.

King James is taking his talents to Philadelphia after what felt like an endless saga of speculation about which team he'll decide to play with in free agency. This marks the fourth franchise James has played for, and the fifth time he has joined a new NBA team during his legendary career.

It seems that singer-songwriter Hilary Duff seems to think this is too much team-jumping from James, which she referenced during her Lucky Me Tour stop at Philadelphia's TD Pavilion Sunday night.

When speaking to the crowd about the cities her tour has stopped at, Duff said, "We started in Florida, went to LA, we've ended up here [in Philadelphia]. I'm starting to feel like LeBron!"

Hilary Duff at her concert last night in Philly:

“We started in Florida, went to LA, we’ve ended up here… I’m starting to feel like LeBron!” pic.twitter.com/nVpDHragPk

Duff did indeed begin her tour in West Palm Beach, Fla., on June 21. She performed at the KIA Forum in Inglewood on July 8 and 9 and was in Philadelphia last night.

The one city James played at that isn't a tour destination for Duff is Cleveland, as the pop singer decided to make a stop at nearby Cincinnati instead.

It would be funny to see what James' reaction to this comment from Duff might be. While it didn't seem malicious, Duff was clearly taking a subtle dig at the four-time NBA champion.

But James won't worry about being the butt of anyone's jokes if he can secure one last championship during his tenure in Philadelphia.

title: Source: Colts WR Alec Pierce received PRP injection to speed up healing in ankle
description: Colts WR Alec Pierce received a PRP injection to speed up the healing process in his left ankle since his late-March surgery
fullText:
Colts receiver Alec Pierce received a platelet-rich plasma injection in his left ankle at some point after he had surgery on his left ankle, a source confirmed to IndyStar on Monday.

It's not clear when Pierce received the injection. He sought out the additional procedure, according to the league source, to help with lingering soreness and speed up the healing process. The injection wasn't due to a setback in his rehab, the source said. Pierce also had a PRP injection prior to surgery.

Pierce, who received the richest free agent wide receiver contract in league history – four years, $114 million -- this offseason, remains on the physically unable to perform list as the Colts prepare for Tuesday's joint practice with the Patriots.

The team is yet to offer a concrete update when the receiver will be back on the field two weeks after general manager Chris Ballard told reporters Pierce was "probably still a week or two away,"

"Not right now," Colts head coach Shane Steichen said when asked Thursday if the Colts had a timeline for Pierce's return. "His rehab is going great, I'll say that. I don't have a timetable on his return, but he's doing a hell of a job on his rehab."

Added receivers coach Reggie Wayne on Sunday: "(Pierce is) upbeat, and if he's upbeat, that means he's where he wants to be and where he needs to be."

Pierce received his second PRP injection this offseason in the four-and-a-half months since undergoing what Ballard called a "clean-up" surgery to relieve the fifth-year wideout of pain that had become a regular presence over the last month of the 2025 season. Pierce told reporters in June that he received a PRP injection days after the end of the season in hopes of avoiding surgery and speeding up his body's natural healing process. Doctors required up to eight weeks to determine the effectiveness of the injection, and though Pierce had begun light jogging by the time he signed his new long-term deal in mid-March, the pain had not subsided.

Doctors told Pierce that surgery was more a "when" than "if" situation – meaning he could put off surgery until immediately after the 2026 season, but waiting would come with heightened risks for injury. Surgery, coming with a four-to-six-month recovery timeline, was the choice in late-March – a move that called into question Pierce's availability to start the regular season.

The message around the Colts continues to be positive with more than a month left in Pierce's initial recovery window.

"Obviously, we know what he means to our (receiver) room," Wayne said Sunday. "But I just want him whenever he's 100%. I don't want him 85%. I don't want him 80%. I need him 100%.

"However long that takes, it is what it is."

Joel A. Erickson and Nathan Brown cover the Colts all season. Get more coverage on IndyStarTV and with the Colts Insider newsletter.

title: Athletics’ Jacob Wilson Sets Unique MLB Record
description: In just his second full season at the major league level, Athletics shortstop Jacob Wilson is already making MLB history.On Sunday night, as the Athletics picked up a series win over the Boston Red Sox, Wilson played in his 111th straight game without recording an error. By doing so, he surpassed former Athletic Mike Bordick’s […] The post Athletics’ Jacob Wilson Sets Unique MLB Record appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
In just his second full season at the major league level, Athletics shortstop Jacob Wilson is already making MLB history.

On Sunday night, as the Athletics picked up a series win over the Boston Red Sox, Wilson played in his 111th straight game without recording an error. By doing so, he surpassed former Athletic Mike Bordick's 24 year old record for the longest errorless streak by a shortstop in the history of Major League Baseball. Bordick set the record at the age of 36 during the 2002 season while a member of the Baltimore Orioles and finished the season with just a single error.

"[I'm] a little surprised that record got broken," Bordick said on MLB Network Radio. "That young man is picking it out there as an Athletic."

"It's a special day for me, but at the end of the day, we got our first series win in a long time against a great opponent," Wilson told MLB.com's Greg Levinsky.

Ironically, Bordick's sole error in the 2002 season was on April 10, 2002, less than two weeks after Wilson was born on March 30. As for Wilson, his most recent error came more than a calendar year ago. He had a single error on July 6, 2025 against the Athletics' Northern California rival, the San Francisco Giants. It was his eighth error of his rookie season.

During the 2026 season, Wilson has had 81 putouts and 128 assists, along with 28 double plays, yet has been perfect to this point.

Wilson, 24, has been limited to just 76 of the Athletics' 118 games this year due to injury, but when in the lineup, he's been one of their  most reliable bats as well. His .269 batting average is the most among any Athletic to appear in more than 70 games to this point in the season and the second-highest amongst any player to appear in more than 20 games, trailing just Zack Gelof's .273 average.

It's been a big year for Wilson, both on and off of the field, as he signed a huge contract extension to stay with the Athletics back in February. His new contract runs through the 2032 season and is worth a total of $70 million. The Athletics also have a team option for the 2033 season, which they'll likely pick up if he continues to develop at this pace.

Wilson has almost certainly entered himself into the conversation for a Gold Glove this season, the only thing holding him back will likely be his low number of games played when the season draws to a close. He'll have to play every inning for the rest of the month to hit the 750 threshold before the Athletics' 138th game to qualify for the award, which may be a tough task.

Wilson has come quite a long way from when the Athletics drafted him sixth overall just three years ago. When healthy, he's been a major bright spot for a struggling team. However, for him to truly show his long-term value to the organization, he'll have to find a way to be on the field more regularly.

title: WNBA to discuss transgender athletes at anti-hate task force meeting
description: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert will meet with multiple team representatives part of the league’s existing anti-hate task force.
fullText:
WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert and multiple team representatives part of the league's anti-hate taskforce will meet this week for ongoing discussions on various topics, including transgender athletes in women's basketball, a person with direct knowledge of the situation told USA TODAY Sports.

The anti-hate taskforce meeting was already scheduled prior to games over the weekend and comes amid a growing national conversation around the league, player safety, race, politics and equality.

Recently, transgender athletes have been in the spotlight after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham openly spoke about "protecting women's sports" through clear gender policies.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" Cunningham said she told ESPN during a February interview that was published July 21. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Multiple "Support Sophie Cunningham" demonstrations have since occurred at Fever games, including as recently as Saturday, Aug. 8, ahead of a road game against the Chicago Sky.

That same day, the Women's National Basketball Players Association (WNBPA) released a statement denouncing transphobia and other forms of hate.

"The WNBPA represents 200+ individual people with different lived experiences, cultures, lifestyles, and opinions. We embrace justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion," the union said. "Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations. But we will not be used as political pawns."

The day before, Engelbert sent a memo to teams addressing conversations around transgender athletes in women's basketball, the Associated Press and ESPN reported.

"I know many of you have received questions in recent weeks regarding transgender athlete participation in women's basketball, and I expect this topic will continue to receive significant attention," Engelbert said in the memo. "I wanted to reach out to share how we are approaching these conversations at the league office and to thank those of you who have responded to questions from the media with thoughtfulness and professionalism."

Engelbert's memo said the WNBA plans to "approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league."

"Second, our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained," she added. "Lastly, preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities."

The league's latest collective bargaining agreement, which was negotiated earlier this year, states "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA." It includes additional eligibility criteria such as age and remaining collegiate eligibility but does not explicitly mention gender identity or gender at birth. The absence of that specificity has been thrust into the national spotlight.

Last week, Vice President J.D. Vance told Fox News he would encourage Cunningham to "keep speaking her mind."

"We cannot take our country back; we cannot save the United States of America unless you have people of courage who are speaking their mind," Vance said on the cable network Aug. 5.

President Donald Trump's administration has enacted sweeping anti-transgender executive orders and federal policy changes, signing Executive Order 14201, titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports," on Feb. 5, 2025.

The directives work to provide a government-wide definition recognizing only two sexes assigned at birth, restrict transgender inclusion in school and college sports under Title IX, target federal funding for gender-affirming care and roll back federal non-discrimination protections.

The wave of anti-transgender legislation is aimed at a tiny portion of the population — 1% of people aged 13 and over in the U.S. identify as transgender, according to a 2025 study by the Williams Institute at UCLA Law.

The Human Rights Campaign reported in 2023 that 19% of transgender youth nationwide were playing sports, including fewer than 1,300 who played sports in school. In 2024, NCAA president Charlie Baker testified to the Senate that he knows of fewer than 10 transgender student-athletes out of 510,000 college athletes.

There are no transgender women playing in the WNBA.

USA TODAY reporter Danielle Lerner contributed to this report.

title: Former Illini set for NFL preseason debuts
description: Several former Illini will take the field this week, making their NFL preseason debuts and beginning their push to earn roster spots.
fullText:
It's the start of the NFL preseason, which means some familiar faces will be making their debuts this week.

The Illini saw three players get drafted in 2026, along with nine others getting scooped up after the fact. Both Gabe Jacas and JC Davis are shoo-ins to make their respective 53-man rosters. However, even big names like Miles Scott and Luke Altmyer will be fighting to prove themselves during training camp.

Before the full preseason slate kicks off, let's take a look at where some former Illini rookies will be playing this August.

After being the last second-round pick to sign their contract, Jacas and the New England Patriots finally inked a deal. Despite dealing with a recurring knee injury, Jacas has stated during camp that he feels 100%. So expect the former Illini star to be lining it up this Thursday against the Colts.

Luke Altmyer will also have his chance to shine on Thursday. Lions Head Coach Dan Campbell said he expects Altmyer to get a lot of snaps against the Bengals.

After a stellar senior season, Altmyer went undrafted this April. It was a surprise to many, but now Luke's opportunity is here, as he will be in a battle to make the regular season roster.

Staying in the NFC, JC Davis will make his debut for the Giants on Saturday.

The offensive lineman went in the sixth round of the draft and is currently second on the left tackle depth chart. Backing up one of the best tackles in the league, Andrew Thomas.

It's a good landing spot for Davis – who will have an excellent chance of not only making the roster but receiving serious playing time this year.

Heading back to the AFC, Miles Scott will also make his debut for the Broncos.

He was the final Illini selected in the 2026 draft, going in the seventh round.

Scott is currently listed as the third-string free safety for Denver. A strong pre-season campaign will be vital for Scott, as he fights to stay on the 53-man roster.

Besides the aforementioned players, more Illini rookies will be beginning their battle to make the final roster this week.

Familiar names include Hank Beatty, Josh Gesky, Josh Kreutz, Dylan Rosiek and Tanner Arkin.

All will have an outside chance of making their teams' 53-man rosters, but the pre-season is the perfect time to show what they are about.

title: Two Things Bear Bachmeier Needs to Improve Upon In 2026
description: This time last year, we were just learning about incoming freshman quarterback Bear Bachmeier. He had transferred from Stanford after spring ball in 2025, having only been with the program for two months leading into fall camp. Over the coming weeks of practice leading up to their opening game against Portland State, more and more […]
fullText:
This time last year, we were just learning about incoming freshman quarterback Bear Bachmeier. He had transferred from Stanford after spring ball in 2025, having only been with the program for two months leading into fall camp. Over the coming weeks of practice leading up to their opening game against Portland State, more and more buzz generated regarding No. 47.

As we know, Bear Bachmeier eventually (and rather emphatically) won the starting job out of camp. Offensive coordinator Aaron Roderick almost seemed to have to restrain himself from praising the true freshman too much. He was giddy. The biggest compliment Roderick gave him was his grasp of the playbook, even while only starting on it a few months before. Certainly, he started at a massive disadvantage from his competitors McCae Hillstead and Treyson Bourguet, who both had significant time in BYU's system before Bachmeier's arrival.

Still, Bachmeier won the job. And played marvelously in 2025, not even just for a freshman, but in general. He was one of the most efficient quarterbacks in the Big 12 Conference. He guided BYU to its fifth ever 12-win season. He earned Big 12 Offensive Freshman of the Year. Finishing fourth in passing yards in the Big 12, he added 11 rushing touchdowns, which were more than all but two players in the entire Big 12, regardless of position. Along with putting up admirable stats, Bachmeier showed wisdom, leadership, and maturity beyond his years, winning teammates and fans over with his demeanor and even musical hobbies off the field.

As the great play-by-play voice Jason Benetti put it last year against Utah, "there is a Bear on the loose in Provo" once again in 2026. Even still, there are a few things Bachmeier can do to take his game to an even greater level in year two.

On passing attempts of at least 20 yards, Bachmeier completed 30.2% of of them last year. Among 76 qualified power conference quarterbacks last year, that ranked 61st. Plus, he had the third-most turnover-worthy throws when targeting at least 20 yards downfield of any of those signal callers. While Bachmeier was excellent in the short and intermediate passing depths, at times he lacked in getting the ball downfield. He completed 13 such attempts last year, which was tied for 11th in the Big 12. For context, the leader was Baylor's Sawyer Robertson, with 30.

Part of that was scheme, of course. Roderick did not want to fully expose his true freshman quarterback to possible turnovers or big hits from pass rushers when waiting for receivers to get downfield. That part can evolve this year, as Bachmeier has earned more trust. This can naturally progress as Bachmeier grows and becomes more comfortable. Clearly, Bachmeier has a cannon arm for it. Look for the Cougars to be more aggressive downfield, especially with a huge receiver in the 6-foot-6 Kyler Kasper in the fold now.

Protecting Himself When Running

Among all Power Four conference quarterbacks, only five had more rushing attempts than Bachmeier. He had the seventh-most missed tackles forced among quarterbacks when running as well. That can take a toll. We saw it down the stretch last season when he played the Pop-Tarts Bowl hobbled after getting injured in the Big 12 Championship Game. Even with Bachmeier's stout frame, that will wear him down over time.

Bachmeier is an excellent runner. His physicality as a runner sets him apart from many other high-level quarterbacks. That's an advantage BYU can use against opposing defenses. However, Roderick and company need to be smarter about how they deploy Bachmeier in the run game. Perhaps he gets out of bounds or slides more often this season to protect himself. He can still pick certain spots where he needs to be physical and lower his shoulder pads. BYU needs Bachmeier to be healthy, plain and simple. There needs to be a bit more of a balance and moderation to his run game in 2026.

title: Isaiah Stewart Reveals Why He Was Ready to Leave Pistons
description: Isaiah Stewart says he was ready for a fresh start after his role with the Pistons dropped dramatically during the playoffs.
fullText:
Isaiah Stewart never hid what Detroit meant to him.

For six seasons, he played like somebody who understood exactly what Pistons fans value. Toughness. Effort. Physicality. No backing down. Yet when his role shrank during Detroit's playoff run last spring, Stewart began wondering whether his future still belonged in the Motor City.

Now, nearly two months after the Detroit Pistons traded him to the Memphis Grizzlies, Stewart has opened up about what was happening behind the scenes.

And his comments make one thing pretty clear: by the time the trade happened, Stewart was ready for a fresh start.

Stewart told ESPN's Marc J. Spears that the hardest part was putting in the work without understanding why his opportunity had changed.

"When things are out of your control, the only thing you can do is pray," Stewart told Spears. "And I was in a situation where you will work so hard and you have a goal, you are putting your all into something, and you're not able to get a certain opportunity or reap that kind of reward.

"You don't know why, and it'll make you question yourself, stress yourself out because of the passion and love you have for the game. We felt all we could do is just pray. Let the Lord figure it out, because he always works things out for us."

That frustration had been building during Detroit's postseason run.

Stewart averaged 22.7 minutes during the regular season, but that number plunged to 11.8 minutes per game in the playoffs. His calf injury earlier in the year naturally created questions about whether health played a role, but Stewart said during the postseason that he was fully healthy.

His explanation then was straightforward.

"I've been available to play," Stewart said in May. "With the minutes, it's the coach's game plan; you have to trust and respect it. All I can do is control what I can control. Obviously, I would love to be out there, but all I can do is trust the game plan and be a great teammate."

There was no public blowup. No trade demand. No attempt to embarrass the organization.

But the disappointment was real.

Detroit's rotation told the story before the front office ever made the trade official.

Paul Reed began taking on a larger role behind Jalen Duren during the playoffs and delivered productive minutes. Reed appeared in nine postseason games, averaged 7.4 points and shot 66.7 percent from the floor.

Once that happened, Stewart's place in Detroit became much less certain.

President of basketball operations Trajan Langdon later explained that Stewart's calf issue and conditioning had contributed to the situation.

"Stew was not hurt. I give him a ton of credit," Langdon said. "He had a suspension going into All-Star (break), he played for four or five games, and then had an injury to his calf. There was some slight deconditioning at the wrong time. I don't think he was at the height of his conditioning, but he came in and gave us what we could at that time."

From Detroit's perspective, there was also a financial component that could not be ignored.

Stewart is owed $30 million over the next two seasons. Moving that contract while acquiring three second-round picks created additional flexibility for a Pistons front office that still has major business to handle, including its unresolved contract situation with Duren.

This was not simply Detroit deciding Stewart could no longer play. It was a roster decision, a financial decision and, increasingly, a role decision all wrapped together.

When the trade finally happened in June, Stewart admitted he did not immediately know how to process it.

"I didn't know how to feel," Stewart told Spears about being traded. "I wasn't mad about it. I was happy that I was moving on to a new chapter.

"At first I was like, 'Man, so first time I got traded in my career, and I'm in Memphis.' New teammates, new guys in the system. My mind just started going that way. And I'm thankful because I'm somewhere where I'm really wanted. And the fanbase already respects and loves who I am. I'd rather be where I'm wanted than headed back into a situation where it's not the best."

That final sentence will get the attention of Pistons fans.

"I'd rather be where I'm wanted."

It is difficult to hear that and not recognize how Stewart viewed the end of his Detroit tenure.

For years, he had been one of the franchise's most recognizable personalities. He survived the rebuilding seasons, the losing streaks, coaching changes, front-office changes and constant roster turnover.

Then Detroit finally became a contender, and Stewart found himself playing his smallest role at precisely the moment the games mattered most.

Stewart played 365 games for the Pistons after arriving in 2020, averaging 8.8 points, 6.8 rebounds and 1.2 blocks.

Those numbers never fully explained his popularity.

Detroit fans connected with Stewart because he played with an edge. He battled bigger centers, protected teammates and rarely treated any possession like it was meaningless.

For a franchise that spent much of his tenure searching for an identity, Stewart always had one.

He also developed a connection with the city that went beyond basketball.

"I have just so much love for the city of Detroit," Stewart told Spears. "They welcomed me with open arms. Coming in at 19, I instantly went to the community just naturally. There are a lot of great people that are doing a lot of great things in Detroit."

That relationship is why his departure feels different from a routine offseason transaction.

Detroit did not merely trade a backup big man. The Pistons moved one of the few players who had been present for nearly the entire climb from the bottom of the Eastern Conference into postseason contention.

The Grizzlies finished just 25-57 last season, so Stewart is not walking directly into a championship contender.

What Memphis can offer is opportunity.

Stewart has already lived through a rebuild once. He knows what losing seasons look like, what young locker rooms need and how quickly the mood around a franchise can change once winning begins.

There is also something fitting about Stewart landing in Memphis.

Few NBA cities appreciate hard-nosed basketball more than Memphis. Stewart's game has never been about finesse first. His value comes from physicality, defense, rebounding and the willingness to make the uncomfortable plays.

If the Grizzlies want players who can help restore some edge to the franchise, Stewart makes plenty of sense.

The Isaiah Stewart trade makes more sense now than it did on the day it happened.

Detroit had reduced his role, found another option in Paul Reed and needed greater financial flexibility. Stewart, meanwhile, wanted a place where his opportunity matched the work he was putting in.

Those two realities eventually reached the same conclusion.

There does not appear to be bitterness toward Detroit itself. Stewart still talks about the city with genuine affection. His disappointment was with his basketball situation and the feeling that his role no longer reflected what he believed he could provide.

That is what makes this one complicated for Pistons fans.

Detroit may have made the right basketball decision.

Stewart may also have been right to want something more.

title: Sky's DiJonai Carrington tries to clarify 'White Privilege' post after ejection, hard foul on Sophie Cunningham
description: Though she said it's unrelated to the foul, DiJonai Carrington did not explain what her "White Privilege" post was intended to mean
fullText:
DiJonai Carrington is trying to clear up her "White Privilege" post on social media.

The Chicago Sky guard was ejected after committing a hard foul on Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham on Saturday. Then, shortly after being thrown out of the loss in Chicago, Carrington took to social media.

She posted "White Privilege" in all caps and tagged the Fever on Threads while the game was still going on. That post, as of Monday afternoon, is still up.

But on Monday, Carrington addressed the post while responding to former NFL linebacker Emmanuel Acho. She insisted that she "never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege."

I’ve never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege (that was your assumption). Try exercising your critical thinking skills, I know you studied psych. Furthermore, I’m the LAST thing from ignorant or asinine when it comes to speaking on “white privilege”,… https://t.co/mykXGTtiXJ

"Try exercising your critical thinking skills, I know you studied psych," she wrote. "Furthermore, I'm the LAST thing from ignorant or asinine when it comes to speaking on "white privilege", do ya research on that one. I actually went to school, one of the top universities might I add, to educate myself on this exact subject. I would never use that term as a rhetorical weapon knowing the historical and social weight it holds without having the proper evidence to substantiate it."

Carrington did not provide an alternative explanation for what her post meant.

Late in the first quarter of Saturday's contest at Wintrust Arena, Carrington whacked Cunningham in the face hard as she went up for a layup. Officials quickly reviewed the play and upgraded the foul to a flagrant 2, which prompted Carrington's ejection.

DiJonai Carrington was assessed a Flagrant 2 and was ejected from the game after this play. pic.twitter.com/WRapu4lqHX

Carrington seemed shocked that her foul was upgraded, which officials said was due to her windup, impact and follow-through, and that there was a high potential for injury with Cunningham in a vulnerable position.

Cunningham and the Fever have been at the center of the WNBA's latest controversy after she spoke about transgender women in sports in an ESPN profile. Rallies have been held outside of Fever away games, too. The team has distanced itself from those rallies and made comments focused on inclusion. Cunningham, after initially doubling down on her stance, has since said she wants everyone to "get back to basketball."

Cunningham was asked about the foul after the game, and said she thought it had nothing to do with race. She did, though, think it was "intentional."

"I've never really spoken to her and have no beef with her, but I guess she has some pent-up stuff," Cunningham said. "So get your s**t off. That's fine, I can take it."

Carrington has averaged 9.8 points and 2.2 rebounds per game this season, her sixth in the league. The Sky, with a 12-20 record, will take on the Seattle Storm next on Monday night.

title: WWE's The Miz has a word for Brewers' Misiorowski on Pat McAfee's show
description: Who is the real Miz? WWE's The Miz crashed Jacob Misiorowski's appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show" to have a word with the Brewers pitcher about his nickname.
fullText:
Two days before he set another pitching milestone in a season of many, Milwaukee Brewers All-Star pitcher Jacob Misiorowski appeared on "The Pat McAfee Show" for a guest spot on Aug. 7.

But soon, another Miz would join the party. And this Miz, the one known for his work inside a wrestling ring, in movies and on reality TV, wanted everyone to know one thing.

WWE's Mike Mizanin, better known by "The Miz," for 20 years, told Misiorowski and McAfee's crew that "I am The Miz, I'm the only Miz, I'm the real Miz."

Upon the wrestler The Miz calling into the interview, McAfee jokingly referred to him as "The Mike."

The wrestler wasn't having any of that.

The Miz, who is one of the best in the business on the microphone, then delivered a promo as if he was appearing on "Monday Night Raw" as the Brewers' ace had a good laugh.

"It is The Miz, the most must-see WWE superstar of all-time. First-ever two-time Grand Slam champion in the history of WWE. Twenty-two titles in my name. That is The Miz."

Mizanin went on to say that he has Google alerts set up for his name, something he started two decades ago when he got his start in WWE. He's still getting them but these days they're not about his championships or the game shows he hosts.

"Now I get, 'The Miz is throwing 106 mph' and I wasn't throwing 106 mph," he proclaimed. "Every time I hear The Miz, I'm like, 'it's not about me.' I like things about me."

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN..

JOINING US NOW THE MIKE 😂😂

"IT IS THE MIZ" ~ @mikethemiz #PMSLive pic.twitter.com/fgnbiK7QIw

WWE's The Miz better get used to seeing more alerts that are about the Brewers' Miz.

Misiorowski, who sports the lowest ERA in baseball, is the frontrunner to win the National League Cy Young Award and has been setting record after record for his pitch speeds during his second year in the big leagues.

The 24-year-old has broken his own record multiple times for fastest pitch ever for a starting pitcher. He holds the record at 105.5 mph, a pitch he threw June 26 against the Chicago Cubs.

Two starts prior, Misiorowski pitched one of the greatest games in franchise and MLB history when he had a complete-game, 15-strikeout, one-hit shutout of the Philadelphia Phillies in a Brewers 6-0 win. The 15 strikeouts are the most in MLB history in a complete-game shutout of 100 pitches or fewer.

More recently, on July 26, Misiorowski set a franchise record with striking out the first seven batters he faced in an 11-2 win over the Colorado Rockies at home.

And on Sunday, Aug. 9, he racked up nine more strikeouts to become the first pitcher to reach 200 this season. He reached that total in the second-fewest innings in MLB history, accomplishing the feat in 129⅓ innings.

Could WWE's The Miz handle the Brewers' Miz?

Mizanin is a passionate Cleveland Guardians fan and has been a regular in the celebrity softball game during the MLB All-Star festivities over the years.

Maybe MLB could set up a matchup next year if schedules align to have the two Miz's meet up on the diamond.

Or maybe we can settle this one like Mike "The Miz" Mizanin knows how. Inside the squared circle.

"It sounds like I need to get on WWE and we need to have a fight about it," Misiorowski joked. "I don't know how the Brewers are going to handle that one."

WWE's The Miz will always have the last word. In a response to "The Pat McAfee Show" posting the video clip of the interview on X, The Miz replied "I am The Miz! The Mike will NOT become a thing!!!!!"

title: Dodgers add Seth Halvorsen, Charlie Barnes to bullpen
description: LOS ANGELES — After two straight days of heavy bullpen usage, the Dodgers called up a few fresh arms ahead of their homestand opener on Monday night against the Kansas City Royals at Dodger Stadium. fullText:
LOS ANGELES — After two straight days of heavy bullpen usage, the Dodgers called up a few fresh arms ahead of their homestand opener on Monday night against the Kansas City Royals at Dodger Stadium.

Seth Halvorsen and Charlie Barnes were called up from Triple-A Oklahoma City. Barnes was not on the 40-man roster so Jonathan Hernández was designated for assignment — opening spots on the 40-man and active rosters — and Kyle Hurt was optioned. Hernández pitched the final two innings on Sunday's loss in Arizona, and Hurt pitched both Saturday and Sunday against the Diamondbacks.

"Those guys were great for us," manager Dave Roberts said Monday of Hurt and Hernández, "but it's just protecting the downside as far as relieving.

The fresh arm express is always ready, though if the Dodgers have their way they won't necessarily need to use many relievers at all on Monday, with Tarik Skubal making his first start at Dodger Stadium since joining the Dodgers. Skubal is averaging 6.04 innings per start this season and has completed six innings in 12 of his 17 starts.

Skubal was pulled in a 2-1 game after only 85 pitches in six innings last Tuesday at Wrigley Field.

"His last start you could argue I could have let him go one more inning," Roberts said Monday, "But I feel this one — we're going to watch intently, but I feel giving him a little more leash tonight."

The Dodgers acquired Halvorsen from the Colorado Rockies on July 20 in exchange for pitcher Nick Frasso and minor league outfielder Landyn Vidourek. Halvorsen did not allow a run in any of his six appearances for Oklahoma City, with two saves, eight strikeouts and two walks in 6 1/3 innings.

Halvorsen last pitched Thursday, with three strikeouts in a scoreless ninth inning, recording a save for the Comets. That was also Barnes' last game pitched for Oklahoma City, tossing three scoreless innings with five strikeouts on 47 pitches.

This is Barnes' fourth stint in the majors this season, with three scoreless innings in relief for the Dodgers and one bulk appearance allowing seven runs in seven innings that was more about resetting the bullpen than anything else. Barnes twice this season has been designated for assignment, cleared waivers and elected free agency, then re-signed on a minor league deal.

title: 49ers may want to sign RB as injuries mount before preseason opener
description: A trio of veteran RBs were all at the San Francisco 49ers facility for workouts or visits leading up to their preseason opener.
fullText:
The San Francisco 49ers brought in outside help at running back Monday, working out veterans Nyheim Miller-Hines and Zamir White while also hosting Blake Watson on a visit, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter.

The timing tracks with San Francisco's depth chart, which has thinned out fast heading into a joint practice and Thursday's preseason game. Christian McCaffrey sat out Monday's practice with tightness, though the team said the star back is fine. Rookie Jordan James is dealing with a broken rib. Isaac Guerendo is also banged up, and Kaelon Black is nursing a minor injury of his own. With four backs compromised in some form, the Niners needed bodies to get through a physical week of practice against another team's defense.

None of the players who worked out are household names, but each has NFL mileage. Miller-Hines, a fourth-round pick by the Colts in 2018, spent five seasons in Indianapolis and has bounced through stops with the Bills, Browns, the Chargers and Saints since tearing his ACL in a 2023 offseason accident. White, a 2022 fourth-rounder out of Georgia, was the Raiders' lead back for stretches before falling out of the Raiders' rotation last season. Watson, an undrafted free agent out of Memphis who ran an unofficial 4.39-second 40 at his pro day, made the Broncos' initial 53-man roster in 2024 and has bounced between the Broncos' active roster and practice squad since.

San Francisco hasn't announced any signings, but adding a body or two before Thursday's game would hardly be a surprise given the state of the room. It's also a reminder of how quickly joint practices can get complicated for the 49ers — in 2024, the team was forced to scrap its joint sessions with the Saints due to a bevy of injuries. ESPN's Nick Wagoner reported the 49ers were concerned they wouldn't have enough players healthy to even practice.

LEROY, Ill. (WCIA) -- Leroy football has long been a family affair, now approaching 50 years under the leadership of first Jim and now B.J. Zeleznik.

This fall, those family connections extend well beyond the sidelines with two sets of twin brothers making up the Panthers' offensive backfield. Quarterback Brett and fullback Matt Helfrich are joined by wings Jimmy and EJ Chaon.

"We have definitely more chemistry on the team being together all the time," Brett Helfrich said. "Me and my brother worked together all summer as well."

Few members of this team are as eager to kick off the season as Jimmy Chaon, who broke his collarbone on the first play of the first game last season.

"It was hard to watch the guys go out there and me not be out there, but I just try to help," Chaon said, cleared to play this season. "Just do what I can from the sideline, help each other out."

Ahead of his 24th year at the helm, Zeleznik knows that the brotherly chemistry is not the only asset the Chaons and Helfrichs bring to the field.

"Any time you've got kids that put as much work in as they put in, they're not going to quit," he said. "They're going to fight till the end. And that's that's all you can ask of them."

EL PASO, Texas (KTSM) — High school football is getting closer in the Borderland, and teams across the region are officially getting back to work.

In New Mexico, teams kick off their seasons Aug. 20, while Texas teams begin their seasons Aug. 27. KTSM's Nine Overtime will also return Aug. 28 with its first episode of the season.

As part of our high school football preview series, we begin with the Eastwood Troopers.

The UIL allowed teams to begin practices Monday, and Eastwood wasted no time getting on the field.

The Troopers held their first practice of the season at midnight, continuing a tradition that has become a staple of the program.

Eastwood is currently practicing on its baseball field while construction continues on the turf at Trooper Stadium. The team is expected to return to its home field Tuesday.

The Troopers are coming off a successful 2025 season, finishing with 10 wins, a District 1-6A championship and a playoff appearance.

Now, Eastwood will look to build on that success with plenty of experience returning on both sides of the ball.

Senior quarterback Kingston Jeffries returns to lead the offense, while junior running back Matthew Ramirez is also back in the backfield. On defense, defensive end Brandon Jury is one of the key returners for the Troopers.

With that experience back, Eastwood enters the 2026 season looking to make another push for a district championship and another playoff run.

"We're just hungry. I think one of the things when you come off success is it's really easy to be complacent, really easy to be satisfied. But I've never felt that from the kids all offseason. I think you'll see an even better team this year." Eastwood football head coach Julio Lopez said.

"We got the best offensive line. They are bigger and stronger. Our receiver group - we moved Bentley De Vries to wide receiver, and he's been good this offseason," Eastwood senior quarterback Kingston Jeffries said. "We have a lot of returning dudes like Jordan Nava. Honestly, every position we have is filled with a lot of skill."

The Troopers open the season Friday, Aug. 28, against Bel Air.

Eastwood's District 1-6A opener is scheduled for Sept. 25 against Eastlake.

fullText:
Evening rain and the threat of lightning forced postponement of the first two quarter-finals at the ATP Montreal Masters on Monday.

The 12-day event, which has been drawing criticism for excessive length, was unable to stage the matches due to weather interruptions that have repeatedly plagued the tournament, which lasts for nearly as long as a Grand Slam.

The planned Monday matches between Spain's Rafael Jodar and Frenchman Arthur Fils and the clash between Italy's Luciano Darderi and American Brandon Nakashima were both rescheduled for Tuesday.

Defending champion Ben Shelton, the fifth seed from the United States, will face Czech Jakub Mensik and Spain's Daniel Merida will play American Learner Tien on Tuesday in the other quarter-finals.

The oddly scheduled Masters is not due to wrap up until Thursday's final, overlapping with the start of the Cincinnati Masters, the last major event before the US Open.

title: Mercedes Russell shares first reaction after joining Indiana Fever
description: Two-time WNBA champion Mercedes Russell opened up about joining the Indiana Fever after the team signed her through a season-ending injury exception.
fullText:
Mercedes Russell shares first reaction after joining Indiana Fever originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Indiana Fever needed frontcourt help after losing Damiris Dantas for the remainder of the 2026 WNBA season. They found it in a player who knows exactly what it takes to win a championship.

Indiana announced Monday that it signed veteran center Mercedes Russell through a season-ending injury exception. Russell joins the Fever after Dantas underwent surgery to repair a torn meniscus in her left knee.

It did not take long for the two-time WNBA champion to feel at home with her new organization.

"Everybody has been so welcoming," Russell told reporters Monday. "Everybody's saying, you know, they're there for anything that I need. So it's been really cool. It's been seamless."

Russell also expressed her excitement about experiencing the energy surrounding the Fever from the home side for the first time.

"It's incredible," Russell said. "The fans show up, they show out. You can definitely feel the energy. I know I've been the opponent, but now I'll be on the good side, I guess is what you call it."

Russell will not be asked to replace everything Dantas brought to the Fever. The two veteran centers have different skill sets, and Indiana will need to adjust its rotation accordingly.

What Russell does provide is size, rebounding and extensive postseason experience behind All-Star center Aliyah Boston. The 6-foot-6 Russell entered the WNBA as a second-round pick in the 2018 draft after a decorated college career at Tennessee. She spent most of her professional career with the Seattle Storm and was part of the franchise's championship teams in 2018 and 2020.

Russell has averaged 4.6 points and 2.8 rebounds across her WNBA career. She most recently appeared in 20 games for the Los Angeles Sparks during the 2025 season, averaging 1.7 points and 1.2 rebounds in a limited role.

Those numbers may not immediately jump off the page, but Russell is not arriving in Indiana to become a featured scorer. Her primary responsibilities will be defending the paint, screening, rebounding and giving Boston valuable opportunities to rest. Her experience could be especially important for a Fever team with postseason expectations.

MORE: Sophie Cunningham reportedly shopping tell-all book amid WNBA controversy

Russell joined the Fever for practice Monday, but Indiana has not announced whether she will be available for Tuesday's game against the New York Liberty.

The timing of her arrival could force the Fever to get her involved quickly. Indiana will play three more games during a five-day stretch after facing New York. That condensed schedule will make it difficult for coach Stephanie White to lean too heavily on Boston or use undersized lineups for extended periods.

Russell acknowledged that learning an unfamiliar system during the season comes with challenges, but she believes her previous experience will help make the transition easier.

"A lot of the terminology may not be too familiar, but basketball is basketball," Russell said. "At the end of the day, you kind of just go out there and play."

The Fever enter Tuesday's matchup with a 20-12 record and a narrow lead in a crowded Eastern Conference race. Washington and Atlanta are each only a half-game behind Indiana, while New York is also within striking distance.

Every rotation decision carries added importance with the playoff race tightening. Dantas' injury created an unexpected hole at a difficult point in the schedule. Russell will now receive an opportunity to help fill it, and her first impression of Indiana suggests she is eager to begin.

"The turnout is amazing," Russell said of the Fever's fan support. "Going from an opponent to now being firsthand, I'm excited."

Russell may not need to wait long for her first chance to experience that support from the other side.

title: Mizzou Cross Country Sets Its Sights on 2026 Season
description: Coach Kyle Levermore laid out a healthy, experienced roster that will push the program to new heights.
fullText:
The wait is almost over. Missouri's head distance coach Kyle Levermore spoke with reporters Monday, Aug. 10, to preview a 2026 season he believes could be the turning point both the men's and women's cross country programs have been building toward.

Unlike most years, the cross country squad has not even had their first practice yet, as the runners return this weekend, with their first official practice next week. Although this is true, their delayed start comes with a silver lining: a fully healthy roster heading into the fall.

"Everyone's healthy, which is great," Levermore said. "That's a huge positive coming into a year, especially coming off the year we had last year. You know, not just the physical growth of the team, from a performance perspective, but I think how much that took, out of everyone emotionally, to come out of that with a fully healthy team, I'm pumped."

Mizzou's turn hosting an NCAA-level stage in Columbia last season left a mark on the program, particularly on the women's side, where Levermore stated the group has turned a new chapter.

"I feel like this is probably the first time since I've been the coach here that we've come into a season returning a whole team of of people that actually know what it takes to be at the national level," Levermore said. "And to be in the top five in the SEC and and we return almost everyone."

Alongside that experience, his athletes have returned as a group that does not need every step of the way mapped out for them from the coaches, but from themselves.

"They've done it before, and I think that takes a little bit of the emotional, unknown part out of it," Levermore said. "It helps them just focus on what actually needs to be done."

Levermore pointed to transfer student Evyn Humphrey, a Wentzville native and recent Tulsa transfer with three years of eligibility. Humphrey managed to qualify individually for nationals last season, which will hopefully provide the Tigers with one of the biggest additions to the program.

"To add someone of her quality into the group, and have had that experience, and have had it in her home state on her home course, even though she was wearing a different uniform, someone like that is huge, you know, to bring into the group," Levermore said.

Beyond the fellow newcomers, Levermore cited returning progress from Kobi Walker, Mirriam Chepkirui, Charlotte Cullen and Rahel Broemmel. Walker enters her season off of a first place finish at the 2026 Gold Coast Airport 5 km, Cullen enters the season with two huge personal bests this summer and Broemmel had a strong summer in Europe, highlighted by a stellar run at the German National Championships.

"We're better than we were coming into last year," Levermore said. "So I don't know what that means for the women's team. I don't know what that ceiling is, but yeah, it's pretty high. And I think that I'm not going to be shy and say we want to give a run at this title on our home course this year."

Mizzou broke a nine-year drought by reaching the national meet last year, but the men's squad did not make the trip. Now, Levermore says the goal is climbing up to the top-three of the SEC and getting both the men's and women's teams to nationals, something the Tigers have not done simultaneously in 27 years.

"We had a really bad day on the wrong day, but that kind of heavy failure is something that sometimes young groups need, and I think on the women's side you have the opposite where they followed the plan. They saw what it took. They got the experience."

Gans Creek will host two meets this fall instead of last year's four, one being the eighth annual Gans Creek Classic, and the other being the notable SEC Cross Country Championships. The team is skipping the Mizzou season opener to instead travel to Ames, Iowa, to preview the course that will host the NCAA Midwest Regional Championships in November.

"The reason we are not hosting the Mizzou opener is because of our preparation," Levermore said. "We need to go see the course at Iowa State for regionals, and so that's the reason for us not hosting that this year."

This will give the Tigers a chance to run the Iowa State course in September, without the pressure of the postseason, before they see it again at regionals.

The Tigers will host the Gans Creek Classic Friday, Sept. 25 in Columbia, and the SEC Cross Country Championships Friday, Oct. 30, also in Columbia. Both meets should give the squad plenty of chances to build momentum, and a chance to show off their talent in front of a home crowd.

With a healthier, more experienced roster than ever, the Tigers have given themselves every chance to make this their breakthrough year.

title: Mikhail Sergachev got left off the NHL’s top 20 defensemen list. Was it deserved?
description: The NHL had a lot of stellar defenseman this season.
fullText:
NHL Network has made it an annual tradition to rank the top players in the league at each position — top 20 for centers, wingers and defensemen and top 10 for goalies. As is the case with virtually everything on social media, the lists are very much up for debate.

Utah Mammoth fans will notice the absence of Mikhail Sergachev from the top defensemen list, which was published Sunday evening.

NHL Network's Top 20 Defensemen Right Now list has a total of: 
• 21 total All-Star Game appearances
• 11 All-Rookie team honors
• Seven Norris Trophies
• Seven Olympic Gold Medals
• Four Calder Trophies
• Two Conn Smythe Trophies
• Six Stanley Cups

What do you think of… pic.twitter.com/lojAgF9y4V

Sergachev placed No. 18 in 2025, so this year's rankings beg the question: Did Sergachev get worse, or did others simply get better?

Here are some factors to consider — some affirming the league's ranking and others refuting it. The conclusion is up to the individual reader to determine.

Sergachev isn't a 75-plus-point guy like the names at the top of the list, but he is consistently just outside the top 10 in points among NHL defensemen.

His point total increased from 53 in 2024-25 to 59 in 2025-26, but his goal total dropped from 15 to 10.

Offensive production is far from the be-all, end-all — especially when talking about defensemen — but the best defensemen in the world contribute at both ends of the ice.

One of the most telling stats in quantifying defensive impact is on-ice goals against — commonly referred to as "OiGA." Like any stat, it has its flaws and it doesn't necessarily tell a whole story, but it does give a good idea of a player's abilities in his own zone.

At even strength, Sergachev allowed 78 goals against in 2024-25 and 75 in 2025-26. Across all strengths, his numbers improved from 110 to 105.

He played one more game last season than he did the previous one, but a combination of transactions and healthy teammates meant his number of on-ice minutes decreased by 39 in 2025-26. On a per-minute basis, Sergachev allowed fewer goals year over year (though the difference is minuscule).

A number of Professional Hockey Writers Association members have noted that this year's Norris Trophy, awarded to the league's best all-around defenseman, was the most difficult decision on the 2025-26 ballot. Some have even said it was their hardest decision on any NHL award ever.

A total of 14 different players got votes and 10 received votes in the top three. That is to say that the league had an abnormal amount of stellar defensemen last season.

Matthew Schaefer took the No. 7 spot on NHL Network's list after unanimously winning the Calder Trophy as the rookie of the year. Moritz Seider (No. 9) and Jackson LaCombe (No. 17) also appeared on the list after not being on it the previous summer.

You'd be hard-pressed to find a knowledgeable hockey mind that thinks any of those guys shouldn't be in the top 20.

Joining Sergachev as 2025 top-20 defensemen who didn't make the 2026 list were Thomas Harley and Gustav Forsling — perhaps more jarring exclusions that Sergachev.

It wasn't long ago that Victor Hedman and Roman Josi were undisputedly among the league's best defensemen. Both still made the 2026 top-20 list, but they both fell significantly compared to last summer's rankings.

Hedman claimed fifth place last year and fell to 18th this time. Josi went from No. 9 to No. 15.

It's not exactly surprising. Hedman and Josi will both be 36 years old by the end of the calendar year. Injuries limited their respective seasons in 2025-26, which makes it harder for them to impact their teams.

Taking over are the likes of Lane Hutson and Jake Sanderson, in addition to the three aforementioned youngsters who debuted on the 2026 list.

Hutson rose from No. 19 to No. 6, while Sanderson went from 13th place to eighth. The next generation of top-tier defensemen is here, and those guys are starting to get recognized as such.

title: The Roboguard Revolution Is Short-Circuiting
description: Knightscope and other robotics companies are rethinking automated security amid canceled contracts. One pivot? Human guards.
fullText:
Robotics companies promise that video-camera-toting security robots can deter and detect crime. But many companies are rethinking the approach after a trail of canceled contracts and questions about whether the artificial intelligence-powered bots are meeting the needs of businesses and local governments.

Proof News found evidence of at least 21 security robot deployments since 2015. We contacted contract holders and combed news articles and determined that at least 13 of those programs have ended. Silicon Valley-based Knightscope secured the most security robot contracts, according to Proof’s analysis, and also suffered the bulk of cancellations.

For example, New York City’s then-Mayor Eric Adams installed a Knightscope robot on the overnight shift at the Times Square subway station, but the program was scrapped when the pilot expired in 2024. City leaders did not respond to Proof News’ questions about why the robot wasn’t renewed. By the end of its assignment, it was reportedly gathering dust in an empty storefront.

Outside Columbus, Ohio, the city of Dublin pulled the plug on a Knightscope robot in May, ending its two-year pilot program after less than 10 months. The city enlisted the robot, dubbed DubBot, to patrol a downtown park, but city spokeswoman Robyn Gray said it “did not fully meet our operational needs,” and failed to identify any criminal incidents or lead to any tickets or arrests.

Sheila Sparks isn’t surprised. Her family has operated Sparks Protection Services near Columbus for more than a decade and said a human touch is essential to de-escalating sticky situations.

“A robot can’t do that,” Sparks said.

Seeking a new path forward in the security industry, Knightscope CEO William Santana Li said the company is forging a new model, combining its robots and AI-powered software with another key ingredient: human security guards. Knightscope announced it purchased Event Risk LLC, a national security guard firm, earlier this year.

Knightscope has incurred net losses since inception in 2013, according to its most recent quarterly filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and had an accumulated deficit of $237 million. Knightscope hopes its pivot to incorporate people will give it a greater share of the physical security market — which the company believes is worth an estimated $230 billion annually.

Li did not respond directly to questions about the disbanded programs, but said in an email, but said in an email, “Technology cannot do everything — and neither can people — but the combination can be very powerful.”

Knightscope and other American-made robotics companies could get a boost from the recent US Federal Communications Commission ban on foreign-made mobile robot imports. Officials cast the move as a national security imperative given the machines’ surveillance capabilities.

But American roboticists are facing more than foreign competition. Robots have long struggled to navigate environments constantly in flux. AI can’t handle the ambiguous situations that security guards and police face daily, said Missy Cummings, a robotics professor at George Mason University and a director at Mason Autonomy and Robotics Center. While AI decision systems perform well in narrow circumstances, she said, they can perform “miserably” as soon as algorithms are outside their training dataset.

“AI and robots for security have had a long, problematic history,” Cummings said in an email, speaking generally. “I do not see this changing anytime soon.”

In 2016, a Knightscope robot deployed at a shopping center in Silicon Valley rolled over a 16-month-old boy's foot. The company apologized for the “freakish accident” at the time, saying in a statement that the robot veered to avoid the child, who ran backwards and directly into the machine. The next year, one flopped into a Washington, D.C. fountain. The company responded with humor, tweeting: “BREAKING NEWS: “I heard humans can take a dip in the water in this heat, but robots cannot. I am sorry.” Li, meanwhile, told the New York Times that the incident was under investigation and a new robot would be delivered free.

When asked about whether contracts remained active, representatives from neither property responded.

Then there was a trial at the San Antonio International Airport in 2024. Spokesperson Ana Flores said its Knightscope robot struggled with badge scanning, communication, and finding its way around. A door alarm would sound, she said, but the robot wouldn’t respond efficiently. Airport leadership opted to not move forward with a one-year, $21,000 Knightscope lease following a one-month test.

Meanwhile, private security is booming. Security officers have proliferated in recent years as cities embrace private guards, who earn an average of about $40,000 a year, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, about half that of police officers.

Robotics companies pitch their autonomous robots — some of which can be equipped with cameras, facial recognition capabilities, and license plate readers —as another set of eyes. They have no family to go home to and are happy to work nights and weekends.

Security robots promise “an alluring form of surveillance as a service,” Andrew Ferguson, a law professor at George Washington University, said in an email to Proof. In some cases their visible video cameras can “deter crime without having to pay a human being a salary,” he said, but it’s not clear that robots prevent or solve crimes better than people.

“They exist as a physical manifestation — a symbol, if you will — that someone is doing something to address potential crime,” Ferguson said. “Robots are a form of security theater, more optics than results.”

Knightscope isn’t the only one seeing interest fizzle.

Officials in Salem, Oregon, powered off their Daxbots after a three-month pilot with the Oregon-based robotics company earlier this year. They had deployed three Daxbot robots to deter trespassing in a downtown parking garage. The robots recorded license plate numbers, captured photos of vehicles violating parking lot rules, and shared data with police.

Complaints about the parkade are “drastically down” since the pilot ended, according to Salem Police Sgt. Trevor Morrison, but it’s unclear if that’s due to traffic-calming devices or “residual results from the Daxbot patrols.” The pilot ended in April, with city spokesperson Nicole Miller citing no additional funding for robot security.

Daxbots have also disappeared in Tempe, Arizona. A viral video of one blue-eyed bot being outwitted by an onlooker who it demanded “leave the premises” made its way to “America’s Funniest Home Videos.” When asked about the contract, the mixed-use campus, IDEA Tempe, did not respond. Daxbot didn’t respond to Proof’s questions about why the Salem and Tempe contracts ended.

Adam Pioth, who posted the video, told Proof that he visited the robots frequently. A few months ago, he noticed the robots no longer shouted he was trespassing. Instead, he said, they would, “stop, look at me, and then just keep going really slow.” And then, he said, they were gone.

“Goodbye my friend,” Pioth wrote on Instagram in March, “and thanks for all the fond memories.”

Daxbot is rolling into another industry: automated sidewalk assessments. Proof identified at least nine cities nationwide that have contracted with the company since last September to send robots cruising sidewalks to check for compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act.

Boston Dynamics is best known for its robotic patrol dogs, which were recently deployed to two World Cup stadiums. After Hyundai bought the controlling stake in the robotics company in 2021, it began pushing to develop mass-produced humanoid robots to work in automotive manufacturing.

Atlas, its humanoid robot, delivered the match ball to the referee during a game in July. But the strategy has also spurred rolling strikes at Hyundai Motor’s Korean assembly plants.

Critics claim police and security robots aren’t proven crime fighters but are effective at one thing: surveillance.

In 2021, the New York Police Department ended its lease for a Boston Dynamics robotic dog and returned it, The New York Times reported, following public outcry. US Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called the tool — which could climb stairs and was equipped with cameras, lights, and a two-way communication system — “surveillance ground drones” being “deployed for testing on low-income communities of color.”

Boston Dynamics did not respond to requests for comment.

“What it’s really doing is building a mass surveillance system that is impossible to hide from,” said Brian Hofer, executive director of the privacy-advocacy nonprofit Secure Justice. “It is not a society I want to live in.”

Steve Rosta, a retired highway patrol officer and co-owner of Direct Approach Security Services in Ohio, said robots’ cameras may act as a deterrent and even catch videos of crimes, but he can’t see a future where the machines are more reliable than a human guard.

“I’m old school,” Rosta said. “Boots on the ground is always better.”

title: Muse Glimmer 30B unsloth GGUF format Q4, Q6, Q8 quantizations
description: We’re on a journey to advance and democratize artificial intelligence through open source and open science.
fullText:
Unsloth Dynamic 2.0 achieves superior accuracy & outperforms other leading quants.

Authors: Meta Superintelligence Lab
Model Release Date: August 2026
License: Apache 2.0

Muse Glimmer is a 30-billion-parameter causal language model with a dedicated perception encoder, distilled from Muse Spark and purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. The model integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use, multimodal understanding, and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally without requiring cloud infrastructure or network access.

Building effective agents requires key capabilities working together to achieve the user’s goals. Muse Glimmer is trained and evaluated on these capabilities:

Muse Glimmer was optimized for local deployment, and designed to run at practical speeds on consumer hardware without sacrificing quality.

Fitting the Model on Your Device. We use quantization techniques to compress the model's weights to approximately 4-bit precision, shrinking the language model to under 20 GB. This leaves enough headroom for the model's KV cache, the perception encoder for image understanding, and the speculative decoding drafter to run simultaneously within a 24 GB or 32 GB envelope. Critically, we validated that this compression introduces minimum to no degradation on agentic tasks.

* Degradation measured using an average on accuracy metrics across 15 common benchmarks

Faster Generation Through Speculative Decoding Muse Glimmer ships with a lightweight "drafter" model based on DFlash, a small companion network that proposes entire blocks of tokens at once. The DFlash block-diffusion model predicts entire blocks of 16 tokens in a single forward pass. The main model then verifies these proposals in parallel, accepting correct tokens and correcting wrong ones. This technique lets Muse Glimmer generate text significantly faster than standard token-by-token generation while producing identical output quality. We provide quantized drafter versions to incur a smaller memory overhead in the release.

title: No, local models will not win
fullText:
Every time a new open-weight AI model is released, people say that local models are the future. Why spend billions of dollars building out datacenters when everyone will just be able to run AI models on their laptops or phones? I think this idea is doomed. No matter how strong open-weight models get, most inference will always happen in AI datacenters.

Local models are never going to be as powerful. I think this point should be obvious: all of the current frontier models (closed and open-weights) are far too big to run on anything but a full GPU cluster in a datacenter. Of course, smaller models are getting more intelligent over time. In a year you might be able to run something about as strong as GPT-5.6-Sol on your laptop. But by then, you’ll think of GPT-5.6-Sol as too weak to be useful.

Many people deny this last point, but it’s true: almost everyone’s revealed preference is to use the strongest available model in their price range. If AI progress had stalled at GPT-4, I think we could have built some very powerful tools around it, but who’d use GPT-4 today? As LLMs have gotten more capable, our expectations around them have grown: we now expect agentic systems to be able to solve more and more problems independently. It’s intensely frustrating when they get confused or stall out. When given a choice, people are going to pick the model that frustrates them less, which is always going to be the bigger, more powerful one.

On top of that, datacenter models are always going to be cheaper. I don’t understand why people keep saying that local models are cheap: it seems to me to be the same mistake people make when they say that driving Uber is “free money” (ignoring the costs of fuel and wear-and-tear on your car). For the setup price alone of a low-end home lab1, you could buy several years of a paid subscription to one of the AI providers. The power costs would come out to around $50-$300 per month, depending on how much inference you’re running: again, the price of a couple more paid subscriptions.

Why are datacenter models cheaper? It’s not because datacenter inference is subsidized: inference is actually fairly cheap. If you’re running the same model locally and in a datacenter, the datacenter model will be inherently more efficient.

The main reason is batching. A GPU can do hundreds of thousands of mathematical operations exactly as quickly as it can do one. However, for a single user’s inference, each new token depends on the result of the previous one, so it can’t be batched2. What can be batched is the inference of hundreds of users together. This costs essentially as much time, power, and heat as just doing inference for one user at a time.

When you’re running your own inference at home, you’ve got nothing to batch — at best you’re running a few parallel AI agents — so utilization is terrible. There’s a lot of potential inference that you’re paying for but can’t use: it’s just being wasted. The only way around this is to get together with some friends and expose your local inference endpoint to them (at which point you’re basically running your own crappy datacenter).

The other reason is that datacenters have larger, more efficient GPUs to work with. The kind of consumer GPUs you’d run local models on are gaming GPUs like the RTX 4090. A datacenter B200, designed for batched AI inference, gets about three times the flops and just under four times the memory bandwidth for the same amount of power3. So between batching and GPU efficiency, you’re using something like ~30x the resources to run your model locally.

Incidentally, this is why I’m suspicious of people who say that local models are good because they aren’t as resource-hungry as those big bad datacenters. If you want to run LLMs efficiently, you should be trying to push as much of your use into AI datacenters as possible! Charitably, what they mean is that we should all be running smaller models — but even then, you should ideally be using small models via, say, the GPT-5.6 Luna API instead of hosting your own model.

Is there a possible world in which local models win? I suppose so. One thing that could happen is that governments could ban the use of AI datacenters altogether: either due to concerns around the danger of AI, or simply bending to public pressure. In that world, local models would be the only game in town.

Alternatively, AI progress might somehow stall for very large models while progressing for small ones. I struggle to imagine how this might happen (barring government intervention, as above), but a world where a 30B parameter model could be a frontier model is a world where local models might be competitive.

Or maybe models get so good that a 30B model is genuinely smart enough to do everything, so nobody really needs a model like Opus or Sol unless they’re trying to solve the Reimann Hypothesis. I don’t really buy this. Models can do frontier mathematical work today while still being not smart enough to refactor large codebases as well as me, so it’s hard to imagine a world where I don’t just want to use the smartest model available.

I do think there will always be a niche for local models. I’m reminded of the surprisingly simple idea behind Thinking Machines’ “Interaction Models” (which OpenAI also does, because it’s obvious): for latency-sensitive applications like voice chat, you have a small, fast model handle the talking, which delegates to a large, slower model for the hard thinking. I wouldn’t be surprised if most AI use in five years is mediated through a local model on your phone or laptop (though in this world almost all the work would still be done via AI datacenters).

Some users will prefer local models even though they’re weaker and more expensive. For instance, being able to steer the model locally might be a killer feature for those users. Others might simply value having total control over their own infrastructure, or have unreliable internet4. If you’re one of those people — particularly if you only chat to the models instead of using them for research or coding — local models are a good choice for you. However, I think this is always going to be a niche group. The majority of users will continue to do their inference through datacenters.

This link is from a year ago — things are significantly more expensive now.

Specifically, the bottleneck is moving the model weights into the GPU, which needs to be done and takes the same amount of time whether you’re doing it for one user’s token or a hundred users’ tokens.

I estimated this with LLM assistance, but you can check the numbers yourself from NVIDIA.

While still having a reliable power supply and enough money to fit out a home inference cluster.

The discussion around AI sycophancy peaked last year, when the “#keep4o” movement was protesting the removal of OpenAI’s most sycophantic model (GPT-4o), and many people were openly slipping into AI psychosis.

title: Cable Pioneer Bob Miron Dies at 89
description: Robert Miron—best known as Bob to the industry—passed away Wednesday at the age of 89. fullText:
Robert Miron—best known as Bob to the industry—passed away Wednesday at the age of 89. His cable legacy spans the operations and programming businesses, having served as Chairman and CEO of Advance/Newhouse Communications and later Chairman of Discovery Communications.

“He helped build companies, forge partnerships, mentor executives and champion innovations that permanently changed how Americans received news, information and entertainment,” the family wrote in his obituary. His children Nomi Bergman and Steve Miron have spent years in the cable industry, currently serving as President of Advance/Newhouse and CEO of the company, respectively.

While he retired in 2010 after a 50-year career in cable, Miron’s presence was felt long after. In addition to advising behind-the-scenes, Miron was frequently seen at industry events such as the Cable Hall of Fame. He was a committed philanthropist, particularly for his beloved Syracuse University. Earlier this week, he was at the grand opening of the Sunny B Wound Care Center at Crouse Hospital, a program made possible by a donation from his daughter and son-in-law, Nomi and Neal Bergman.

The family memorial quotes Brian Roberts, Chairman and Co-CEO of Comcast, describing Miron as “the consummate gentleman” and “the moral conscience for an entire industry for over five decades.”

John Malone, Chairman Emeritus of Liberty Media, first met Miron through the NCTA board. The two would become partners on some of the industry’s biggest transactions, including helping cable entrepreneur John Hendricks get Discovery off the ground and later the creation of Charter Communications.
