title: Magnitude 7.4 quake rocks western Colombia, killing at least 111 people
description: A powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 111 people, damaging hundreds of buildings and leaving many trapped under debris while their loved ones and resc...
fullText:
CALI, Colombia (AP) — A powerful 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 111 people, damaging hundreds of buildings and leaving many trapped under debris while their loved ones and rescue workers searched through rubble.

Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country's third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers.

"Our building has basically been left in ruins, and the building next to ours? Completely collapsed," said Álvaro López, who cradled his dog as he watched the search. The desperate scene recalled the searches still ongoing in neighboring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by two powerful earthquakes.

Besides Cali, the quake ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales, and was felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. The epicenter was in San Jose del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles (400 kilometers) west of Bogota, the U.S. Geological Survey said.

Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella said at least 87 people were injured and around 1,600 buildings were damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed. He declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery.

"We aren't going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination," he said.

Colombia's Geological Service said Monday's quake was the country's strongest recorded "in the 21st century," and that it was followed by several aftershocks.

Colombia's Pacific region around the epicenter lies along the "Ring of Fire," the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur. The Pacific, particularly the Choco region, is one of Colombia's poorest, nestled in dense jungle. Much of Choco is only reachable by boat or plane, which may pose difficulty in assessing the wider toll.

Local authorities said the death toll included at least 40 people who were killed in the Risaralda region, where Pereira is located, and 27 people in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children. Authorities also confirmed nine people killed in Choco, two in the Caldas region and a 73-year-old in the Antioquia region. It was not immediately clear where the other 32 people died.

The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighboring Venezuela in late June, destroying hundreds of buildings and killing more than 6,300 people.

Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed. Residents and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors. The local government said that people remained trapped in a number of the city's 380 damaged buildings.

"My entire house shook. I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake," he said. "We're thanking God we're alive."

Little was known about the extent of the damage in Choco, a remote region where officials reported dozens of injured people and damaged buildings but few other details. Phone signals were out in many parts of the region's capital, Quibdo. The town closest to the earthquake's epicenter, San Jose del Palmar, has no airport, and is located on top of a mountain ridge along a highway linking the cities of Cali and Pereira.

In Pereira, further south in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, photos and videos on local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling onto travelers taking shelter and screaming. People ran through rubble and plumes of dust, and residents said collapsed stores, residential buildings and homes lined the city. Pereira Mayor Mauricio Salazar told a local radio station there were at least 15 collapsed buildings where people were feared trapped.

In nearby Manizales, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks. Authorities said flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, Buenaventura and Pereira as they assessed damage.

Small earthquakes, known as "temblores," are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare. In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia killed more than 1,100 people.

Response to the earthquake presents the first major challenge for de la Espriella, a Trump ally who was sworn in as president over the weekend. A divisive figure because of his pledge of an all-out crackdown on criminal groups, de la Espriella said he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency.

On Monday night, the U.S. State Department announced it would provide $15.5 million for emergency shelter, food and other earthquake response aid. Governments across Latin America also lined up to help.

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum — whose countries were among the largest providers of aid to Venezuela following its recent crisis — said they were ready to assist Colombia.

"From El Salvador, we are in communication and ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary," Bukele said.

Chilean President José Antonio Kast said Chile, one of the region's most earthquake-prone countries, "knows the pain and the challenge left by earthquakes" and pledged help.

Suárez reported from Bogotá and Janetsky reported from Mexico City. Associated Press journalists Manuel Rueda in Bogotá, Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations and Matthew Lee in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Rockets face nervous wait after defeat by Brave
description: Trent Rockets face a nervous wait to see if they will qualify automatically for the final of The Hundred after a six-wicket defeat by Southern Brave.
fullText:
The Hundred men's competition, Trent Bridge

Trent Rockets 158-5 (100 balls): Santner 35* (23); Worrall 1-21

Southern Brave 159-4 (97 balls): Stubbs 52* (28); Harrison 2-32

Southern Brave won by six wickets

Trent Rockets face a nervous wait to see if they will qualify automatically for the final of The Hundred after a six-wicket defeat by Southern Brave.

The Rockets were unable to defend their total of 158-7 as Tristan Stubbs' unbeaten half-century helped already-eliminated Brave seal a tense victory with three balls to spare.

Sunrisers Leeds could pip the Rockets, who they currently trail by four points, to top spot if they beat Manchester Super Giants at Old Trafford on Tuesday.

Should both sides finish level on 24 points then positions will be determined by net run-rate, with the Sunrisers (1.094) better-placed than the Rockets (0.740).

Sciver-Brunt cameo helps Rockets into Hundred final

Stubbs and Marcus Stoinis were instrumental in pulling off the chase as they shared a 70-run stand for the fourth wicket.

Aussie all-rounder Stoinis whacked four fours and three sixes to make 46 off 25 balls before he miscued a full toss from Ben Sanderson in the penultimate set and was caught.

However, with eight needed off the final five balls, bowled by Lewis Gregory, Stubbs and Nikhil Chaudhary got Brave over the line.

Stubbs sealed the win by whacking Gregory over square leg for six as he finished unbeaten on 52 from 28 balls, having also struck four fours and three sixes at a strike rate of 185.71.

The Rockets had earlier posted what looked a competitive total with the top order all chipping in with useful contributions.

Mitchell Santner top-scored with an unbeaten 35 off 23 balls as he shared an unbroken sixth-wicket stand with Gregory (28 not out off 18 balls) worth 66 runs.

The wickets were shared between five bowlers, with Brave skipper Chris Jordan curtailing Finn Allen's attacking innings on 23 with a superb yorker.

It was a chastening day for 17-year-old quick bowler Manny Lumsden, though, as his first set disappeared for 19 runs and he was not called upon again.

There's plenty on the line at Old Trafford on Tuesday when Manchester Super Giants host Sunrisers Leeds.

Whoever wins the women's match (15:00 BST) will secure a spot in the Elminator against Southern Brave - a tie or no result would see the Super Giants go through.

In the men's match at 18:30 the Sunrisers are eyeing automatic qualification for the final with victory over the Super Giants by a sufficient margin to give them top spot via a superior net run-rate.

The Super Giants need to win themselves to keep alive their own hopes of making the Eliminator.

title: Team GB claim relay golds at European Championships
description: Team GB secure three medals on the opening day of the European Aquatics Championships in Paris, while Jack Kelly sets a new Irish record to reach the breaststroke final.
fullText:
Team GB secured three medals on the opening day of the European Aquatics Championships in Paris.

The men's and women's 4x200m freestyle relay teams both collected gold, while Max Litchfield took bronze in the men's 400m individual medley.

James Guy, Duncan Scott, Matt Richards and Belfast's Jack McMillan came home first in the men's 4x200m relay final.

The quartet were first to touch home in a time of seven minutes 1.52 seconds, finishing ahead of France in second and Germany in third.

In the women's final, Freya Anderson, Leah Schlosshan, Abbie Wood and Freya Colbert powered into first place with a time of 7:45.93.

Hungary were second in 7:49.09, while Neutral Athletes B took bronze in 7:49.13.

Litchfield had to settle for third in the final of the men's 400m individual medley, finishing in 4:11.58.

Ilya Borodin claimed gold with a championship record of 4:08.17, while Italy's Alberto Razzetti was second in 4:10.40.

Jack Kelly twice broke the Irish 100m breaststroke record on Monday to reach Tuesday's final in Paris.

The New York native, who is Irish qualified through his mother, broke the record previously held by Darragh Greene in Monday's heats with a time of 59.27 but bettered that in the semi-final with a finishing time of 58.90.

Kelly finished second in the race behind Italy's 2024 Olympic champion Nicolo Martinenghi in 58.67.

"To go under 59 has always been a dream of mine and to actually see it on the board is just like 'wow," said 23-year-old Kelly.

"It's been an awesome start to the meet and I'm excited to see what I what I do next.

"It was exciting, the energy was there and to feed off it was what I did, it's been a really cool environment. I can hear the guys, they've been very supportive, we're very close and I couldn't wish for better teammates; the environment is great and something that is really cool to be part of.

"Tomorrow I'm going to take it out and go full throttle, that's my thing in the 100 and see what I got."

In the second semi-final, Great Britain's Adam Ramsay-Peaty, who won silver at Paris 2024, came home first in 58.94, with his Team GB team-mate Filip Nowacki second in 59.03 - a 100m record for a Jersey swimmer.

The 100m breaststroke final will take place on Tuesday at 17:48 BST.

Meanwhile, a personal best was not enough for Belfast's Lottie Cullen to secure her place in the 200m backstroke final.

The National Centre Ulster swimmer, representing Ireland, finished sixth in her semi-final with a time of 2:12.22.

title: Ingebrigtsen returns from 'lowest of lows' to clinch 5,000m gold
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen fights back from "the lowest of lows" to win a stunning 5,000m gold at the European Championships after almost a year out with injury.
fullText:
Jakob Ingebrigtsen fought back from "the lowest of lows" to win a stunning 5,000m gold at the European Athletics Championships after almost a year out with injury.

The Norwegian great underwent Achilles surgery in January and only returned to training six weeks ago.

However, 324 days after he last took to the track, Ingebrigtsen produced an astonishing late surge to claim victory.

The 25-year-old clocked 13 minutes 15.29 seconds to win a record-equalling seventh gold at these championships, moving level with Croatian discus thrower Sandra Elkasevic.

"With 600m to go, I knew I was going to win. I was just hoping I was not going to get too tired," Ingebrigtsen told BBC Sport.

"I doubted myself every day and every minute leading up to the last lap, but I am always hoping.

"Coming from the lowest of lows to be European champion again means the world to me. Not even I believed it could happen coming here."

GB's Hunt wins European 100m gold

European Athletics Championships: Key events, timetable & BBC coverage

Ingebrigtsen's last competitive race was at the World Championships in Tokyo last September.

He finished 10th in the 5,000m final, having lined up as the two-time defending champion despite his Achilles issue preventing him from competing during the outdoor season.

Announcing his return at the European Championships in Birmingham, Ingebrigtsen wrote: "If you're waiting for the perfect preparation, perfect conditions, perfect timing, you'll be waiting your whole life."

He said, following discussions with his team, that there was "no reason not to race", suggesting that while he was back to full health, he was not necessarily in shape to compete for his latest continental title.

He did not make it easy for himself. After a slow start, Ingebrigtsen began to make his way through the pack but seemed to be stuck behind France's Jimmy Gressier on the final lap.

However, he was able to wrestle his way through before producing a superb sprint finish to keep his pristine European record intact.

Paula Radcliffe, the former women's marathon world record holder, described it as "a textbook example of how not to run in your comeback race".

"I can't put into words how hard it is for Jakob to come back after that surgery he has had," she said on BBC TV.

"You cannot write off that man."

A two-time Olympic and world champion, Ingebrigtsen has never been beaten at the European Athletics Championships, including winning each of the past four men's 5,000m golds

He has won gold in his past 12 European finals on the track since 2019, when he had to settle for indoor 1500m silver - his only defeat in a European track final.

title: I burned out and quit my demanding career. It turned into an unexpected, 18-month career break that changed my life.
description: Alice Kim quit her finance career due to burnout and found renewed purpose and balance through surfing and freelance work.
fullText:
Alice Kim left her investment banking career after six years of burnout.

During her career break, she started surfing and almost burned out doing the hobby she enjoyed.

Kim realized the mindset that was causing her burnout and is working on correcting it.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alice Kim, a freelancer from Southern California. It's been edited for length and clarity.

I think I was burned out for the entire six-year period I worked in investment banking and private equity. For the first half of my career, I was fresh out of college and felt like I had unlimited grit to push through, but the burnout accumulated over time.

After moving across various roles, ending up in what I'd previously considered to be a dream role with more work-life balance, and still feeling too exhausted to complete the simplest of tasks, I knew something needed to change.

I quit my job, thinking I'd just need a few months to recover; I was so wrong.

I went through a lot of ups and downs, feeling like I was recovering from burnout, only for the feelings to come back. I learned the hard way that it wasn't my job burning me out; it was my mindset keeping me in a cycle of burnout.

After 18 months, I'm ready to go back to work, but I'm choosing a different path.

I entered the industry because it was prestigious, well-paying, and would give me a lot of optionality for my future. There were aspects I enjoyed, like the people and, as lame as it sounds, building Excel models, but it was a lot of work.

Working 80 hours a week or more in a high-pressure environment felt like a recipe for burnout, and as a perfectionist, it was a standard I continuously held myself to. I was functioning on five hours of sleep, staring at screens all day, and drinking so much caffeine to keep me going.

I tried to work out when I could, but I couldn't maintain any healthy habits with the sheer amount of time I was working. On top of it all, the chronic stress made me incredibly impatient and irritable.

My burnout manifested in a sense of dread. The feeling that I was stuck in cement and unable to get myself to do anything or feel motivated. That was really tough for me because I've always identified as an extremely hard worker, and when I couldn't find the willpower to push through, it felt like I'd lost myself.

The decision to leave was gradual, and then really fast. I discovered surfing very randomly on a last-minute trip I took using PTO, and I fell in love with it. It inspired me to start traveling as frequently as I could for surfing, and I realized how sheltered I'd been in my finance bubble.

I had a growing desire to take a career break, and as my burnout grew, I considered it more seriously. I stumbled upon a surf trip to a bucket-list location, and I treated it as my sign from the universe to submit my resignation.

The next day, I booked the trip and planned my exit.

When I first left, I planned exactly four months of travel and decided I'd come back and look for an adjacent role in a similar industry.

As soon as my travels began, I knew four months wasn't going to be enough. I felt happy, and I really felt like it would take longer for me to recover from burnout and feel ready to go back to work.

About six months into my career break, I took up a freelance opportunity and immediately felt burned out again. I think part of the reason my burnout returned was because I went back to work. I felt pulled to work because I needed to be productive to feel valuable.

I was burned out at my new job, but I later realized it was my core belief system that was driving me to act in ways that burned me out. My mentality didn't change just because I rested for a while.

Additionally, because I didn't have my corporate job as an outlet for my perfectionism, I transferred it to surfing. I started pushing myself so hard and holding myself to such high standards that I almost burned out from surfing as well.

I realized the toxic ways I operated were why burnout followed me wherever I went, regardless of whether I had a job.

I've had to deconstruct the belief that my worth comes from work by questioning it and slowly realizing how unrealistic it was. As long as I held those ideas to be true, the burnout would persist.

I still haven't fully deconstructed those thoughts, but each day I get 1% closer. Although my corporate experience wasn't perfect, I'm grateful it provided me with the financial ability to continue my travels while getting my freelance work up and running.

At the beginning of 2025, I pretty much ditched the idea of returning to corporate unless I become extremely desperate. My new goal is to build a portfolio career that aligns with who I am, allows for freedom, and leverages my professional experience.

I'm currently doing strategic finance freelance work while building my social media platforms on the side.

I know I'm asking for a lot to be able to work remotely across different time zones, but that's the goal. I've been making sacrifices for it, like working odd hours to overlap with US business hours, and it's worth it to me.

title: Why has Araujo joined Liverpool and where did it go wrong at Barcelona?
description: Ronald Araujo has joined Liverpool on loan from Barcelona. We explain why Liverpool moved for the Uruguay defender and what went wrong at Barcelona.
fullText:
Barcelona captain Ronald Araujo has arrived in Liverpool after joining the club on season-long loan, with the move including an option for the Reds to make the deal permanent for 55m euros (£47.1m).

For the Premier League side, it's an opportunity to bring in an experienced defender at a crucial time. For Araujo, it's a chance to make a fresh start away from Barcelona.

New Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola gave the move the go-ahead last week and spoke to Araujo via phone, before the Uruguay international travelled to England. Araujo has taken a pay cut for the coming season and Liverpool will cover his salary for the duration of his loan spell.

The structure of the deal reflects Liverpool's need to solve an immediate problem rather than make a long-term commitment - at this stage.

They wanted a defender who could operate both at centre-back and right-back, and Araujo's versatility and physical profile made him an attractive option.

The timing is particularly significant. Conor Bradley, Joe Gomez and Giovanni Leoni are all injured, while new signing Jeremy Jacquet has yet to feature in pre-season.

With Ibrahima Konate leaving for Real Madrid in the summer, Virgil van Dijk is Liverpool's only fit senior centre-back, making the need for reinforcements increasingly obvious.

Liverpool still believe that their stock of centre-backs will serve them well for the coming season and beyond. Jacquet, Leoni, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe are all emerging players in the position.

But Araujo, with his strength, pace and experience at one of Europe's top clubs, was viewed as a player capable of helping Liverpool through that period. His leadership capabilities were also seen as a positive factor. He will wear the number 33 shirt.

At Barcelona, not only did his acceleration allow them to defend a high line with confidence but, at 6ft 4in (1.93m) tall, his frame made him a formidable presence in physical contests and aerial duels.

Araujo joined Barcelona from his native Uruguay in 2018, made his first-team debut the following October and has since gone on to make more than 200 appearances for the Catalan club.

He finished last season as captain, making 38 appearances for Hansi Flick's side in the 2025-26 campaign.

"He is a very good person and an exceptional player, but our style of play is slightly different," Flick said in a recent press conference.

"He is a footballer with great speed and power, and he is good with the ball at his feet, too. I wanted to get him involved; I think he is eager to try new things, and I believe he has also been affected by what happened in the past.

"I said goodbye to him this morning and saw that he was happy. Liverpool is a great club, and I wish him the best. You have to accept it."

The "past" Flick may have been referring to includes a number of high-profile moments in which Araujo's mistakes came under intense scrutiny.

His red card against Paris St-Germain in the 2024 Champions League quarter-finals became one of the defining moments of his Barcelona career, with his dismissal helping turn the tie in PSG's favour.

He was also heavily criticised for mistakes in the second leg of the 2025 Champions League semi-final defeat by Inter, when Flick came out and publicly defended him.

Last season, in Barcelona's Champions League 3-0 away defeat by Chelsea, he was sent off just before half-time after receiving a second yellow card for a foul on Marc Cucurella.

A week after, he was granted a leave of absence to prioritise his mental health and received professional support and treatment to "take care of himself emotionally".

He returned a month later and made 23 appearances over the second half of the season, starting six matches.

There is also a financial benefit for Barcelona.

The club have been looking to generate a significant sale to help ease their financial pressures and, although this is only a loan with an option to buy, Liverpool will cover Araujo's full salary for the season. As one of Barcelona's highest earners, that represents a significant saving for the Catalan club.

For Araujo, though, he arrives at Anfield with an opportunity to reset his career and rediscover the confidence that once made him one of the club's most highly regarded defenders.

title: It's football, not PlayStation - Uefa refs' chief on VAR
description: Uefa referees' chief Roberto Rosetti says some video assistant referee reviews "were not connected with football".
fullText:
Uefa referees' chief Roberto Rosetti says some video assistant referee reviews "were not connected with football" after meeting with leaders from the top European leagues last month.

Rosetti was speaking as he launched Clear Line,, external a first-of-its-kind portal for fans which tries to lay out when a VAR should, and should not, intervene.

The lead referee officers from England, Spain, Germany, France and Italy met with Rosetti and David Elleray, the Ifab's technical director, to try to find a more uniform approach to decisions.

"We realise that everywhere now there is not any satisfaction about how VAR is impacting football," Rosetti said.

"So we want to avoid microscopic situations. The context is super important. It's football, not PlayStation. We need to be very, very careful.

"The referee must referee the match. It's something important for football, for clear situations and clear mistakes."

Only use VAR when error blatant - referee chiefs

Rosetti conceded that trying to find a consistent approach across all leagues, which tend to have their own interpretations of some offences, would be difficult.

In particular, handball continues to cause issues across football.

The Premier League had the most relaxed interpretation of handball last season, with a handball penalty every 17.27 games.

Then came the German Bundesliga at 10.93 games per handball penalty, the Spanish La Liga on 10.56, the Italian Serie A on 10.00 and the French Ligue 1 at 9.27.

In the Champions League, it was a penalty every seven games - the highest frequency in Europe - which highlights the difficulty in reaching a consensus across competitions.

On Clear Line, Uefa has uploaded many video examples of handball situations to explain what is considered an offence.

"The idea is to be more consistent in the application of the laws," Rosetti said

"The perception about handball in England is different. Football is not perfect, and sometimes we will continue to have similar situations interpreted in different ways. But at least we are working together."

With VAR, too, the Champions League and the Premier League are worlds apart.

In the 2025-26 campaign, the Premier League had the lowest intervention rate in Europe at 0.29 per game, while the Champions League was 0.47 per game.

Rosetti said that there were "too many reviews" and more interventions were affecting player behaviour, with attempts to play for or earn video decisions.

"We wanted to come back to the origin of VAR," Rosetti said, referencing incidents like Diego Maradona's 'Hand of God' goal for Argentina against England at the 1986 World Cup.

"We are not happy any more about this kind of use of VAR.

"We want to try to come back a little bit, and to put again the referees at the centre."

Rosetti said that the time being taken over VAR reviews was a particular concern, with lengthy reviews featuring multiple TV replays being less acceptable to supporters.

Any check longer than 90 seconds, Rosetti says, risks "losing credibility".

A new collective protocol was agreed whereby, when at the monitor, a referee would be shown a freeze-frame for point of contact, followed by half-speed, and then full speed for the intensity of the challenge.

"We like referees with personality, taking decisions on the pitch, and VAR intervening only for clear and obvious situations," the Italian said.

"So clear images without too many replays. It is something that for us is very important.

"We were seeing that some on-field reviews were not connected with football. It's about normal speed, context. It's about football."

Rosetti described Clear Line as "a guide for all the people of football" and not for officials.

It goes through each area the VAR covers - penalties, red card, attacking offences, factual decisions and mistaken identity - in great detail with video examples.

"We started to think how we could help everyone to understand VAR better," he said.

"It's a library, a structure, a document where we explain when [and] how VAR will intervene.

"This is not a web page for referees. This is the space that we would you to go to after a Champions League match to check how an incident compares with this library.

"It's for the clubs, for the players, for the fans."

title: US 1500m champion Koech gets three-year doping ban
description: American middle-distance runner Jonah Koech is banned for three years for blood doping.
fullText:
American middle-distance runner Jonah Koech has been banned from the sport for three years for blood doping.

The US Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) said Koech's doping violation was identified after "highly atypical blood values in his athlete biological passport (ABP)".

An ABP tracks an athlete's blood values over time to identify signs of doping even without a positive drug test.

Koech had emerged as the surprise winner in men's 1500m at the US Outdoor Championships last year, finishing ahead of Ethan Strand and 2024 Olympic gold medallist Cole Hocker in a meet record three minutes 30.17 seconds.

His title has now been stripped after the 29-year-old accepted the ban "for the use of a prohibited substance and/or method", USADA said.

It added: "Koech has been disqualified from all competitive results obtained on and subsequent to 30 July 2025, the date of his first abnormal blood sample, including forfeiture of any medals, points, and prizes."

Koech's blood samples were collected before and after the US Outdoor Championships on 30 July and 8 August last year.

He has not raced since finishing 13th in the 1500m final at the World Championships in Tokyo last September.

Born in Kenya, Koech competed collegiately in the United States from 2015 to 2019 before becoming eligible to represent the country in June 2021.

title: Carrington tells critics to do 'research' over 'white privilege' post
description: Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington has told her critics to do their "research" amid the ongoing furore from her on-court confrontation with Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham.
fullText:
Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington has told her critics to do their "research" amid the ongoing furore from her on-court confrontation with Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham and subsequent social media post.

Carrington was ejected from her side's WNBA defeat for committing a hard foul on Cunningham, and then posted "white privilege" on social media tagging Indiana Fever.

Her actions have been heavily criticised by several American sports analysts, including former NFL star Emmanuel Acho.

On the Speakeasy - Podcast, Acho said: "It was not a race-based decision. To call that a white privilege-based foul is to completely undermine the term of white privilege and to also completely ignore the rules in basketball.

"You hit her in the head. You drew blood. You didn't connect with the ball at all whatsoever. So to me, it was just very ignorant and, to some degree, asinine by DiJonai Carrington to suggest that that call was based on white privilege."

However, that has prompted Carrington, 28, to issue a response on social media, external although she is yet to fully explain the meaning of her post in the aftermath of the game.

Writing on X Carrington, said: "I've never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege [that was your assumption].

"Try exercising your critical thinking skills, I know you studied psych.

"Furthermore, I'm the last thing from ignorant or asinine when it comes to speaking on 'white privilege', do ya research on that one. I actually went to school, one of the top universities might I add, to educate myself on this exact subject.

"I would never use that term as a rhetorical weapon knowing the historical and social weight it holds without having the proper evidence to substantiate it."

Asked about the post after her team won 90-86, Cunningham said: "I think the league is taking care of that.

"This has nothing to do with race. Last year, I did the same thing and I got kicked out, and I deserved to be kicked out. There's no reason even to play that card."

title: Forest owner Marinakis sues Palace over gun banner
description: Evangelos Marinakis is suing Crystal Palace for a banner unfurled by their fans depicting the Nottingham Forest owner holding a gun to midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White's head.
fullText:
Evangelos Marinakis is suing Crystal Palace for a banner unfurled by their fans depicting the Nottingham Forest owner holding a gun to midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White's head.

Marinakis' lawyers lodged the defamation claim in the High Court on Monday, with CPFC Limited listed as one of the two defendants.

The banner, seen during a 1-1 Premier League draw between the two sides at Selhurst Park last August, read: "Mr Marinakis is not involved in blackmail, match-fixing, drug trafficking or corruption."

Marinakis has consistently denied any wrongdoing in relation to such allegations.

In November 2025, the Football Association had charged Palace with failing to ensure that supporters did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or provocative way.

While the banner was not specified as the reason for the charge, there are strict rules regarding messaging containing defamatory, political and offensive slogans.

England international Gibbs-White had come close to leaving Forest last summer after Tottenham appeared to trigger a £60m release clause.

But he signed a new contract to stay at Forest and spoke about his decision during an interview alongside Marinakis.

Marinakis-owned Forest had taken Palace's place in the Europa League last season after the south London club were relegated to the Conference League for breaking Uefa's multi-club ownership rules.

title: GB's Hunt comes of age with European 100m gold
description: Britain's Amy Hunt has her "coming of age" moment as she storms to 100m glory at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham.
fullText:
Amy Hunt had her coming of age moment as she stormed to 100m glory to claim her first senior international title and deliver Britain's first gold medal of the European Athletics Championships.

Hunt announced herself on the sport's global stage last year with world 200m silver in Tokyo - the first individual international medal of her senior career.

Having backed that up with Commonwealth 100m silver two weeks ago, the 24-year-old would not be denied gold this time in Birmingham.

"I have had such a string of silvers and I was starting to get a bit fed up with it, so I thought it was time for gold," Hunt, who won in 11 seconds flat, told BBC Sport.

"My parents gifted me these gold earrings to finally level up, because I wear all-silver jewellery.

"They said it was time for gold - they left me that note two nights ago - so it made me quite emotional.

"It was definitely time for me to come of age here."

It was Britain's second medal on the opening day of action after the hosts took silver in the mixed 4x400m relay.

Yemi Mary John held off Dutch athlete Myrte van der Schoot on the home straight to bring a British quartet also featuring Ben Jefferies, Charlotte Henrich and Toby Harries home in three minutes 10.47 seconds, behind winners Norway (3:09.62).

Hunt's breakthrough individual medal last September was a long time coming, but the early years of her senior career were disrupted by injury as she sought to balance the demands of training with studying for an English Literature degree at Cambridge University.

Before those challenging years, Hunt set a women's under-18 200m world record in 2019 - breaking Asher-Smith's British under-20 record in the process - but it would be six years before she managed to improve on that personal best time in her favoured event.

Hunt also ruptured her quad muscle in 2022 but, with those setbacks now behind her, continues to make exciting progress under the guidance of coach Marco Airale in Italy's northern city of Padova.

Now consistently able to produce personal-best performances, the silverware is beginning to follow - and this golden moment signalled a changing of the guard at the top of British sprinting.

Discussing her ambitions before the championships, Hunt quoted High School Musical character Sharpay Evans, who sings a song called "I Want It All" in the film.

Full of confidence after breaking the 11-second barrier for the first time earlier this season, she raised her arms in celebration after producing a trademark strong finish which delivered her from fifth to first over the second half of the race.

"I want it all and I'm someone who doesn't shy away from what she knows she can do," said Hunt.

"I knew I could come away with gold. I had such a big premonition."

Ingebrigtsen clinches 5,000m gold on injury return

European Athletics Championships: Key events, timetable & BBC coverage

Hunt could have as many as three opportunities to add to her tally this week, as se competes in the 200m and both the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events.

Typically not the quickest off the blocks at almost six-foot tall, Hunt was seventh in the eight-athlete final after the first 10m.

But she held her form superbly to overhaul her rivals and end her wait for gold, just two years after finishing seventh in the previous European final in Rome.

"I just had such a magical feeling," Hunt said.

"I've won English Schools here, raced here as a 13, 14-year-old. I just had a feeling that this was going to be my night.

"My first gold. I think it was definitely time for an upgrade, and I'm now kind of fully established."

British record holder Asher-Smith lined up in Birmingham as the defending champion - but the 30-year-old could not force her way into medal contention.

Asher-Smith, bidding to win a historic seventh gold and become the joint-most successful athlete in the history of the championships, finished fifth in 11.10, as Poland's Ewa Swoboda (11.02) and Belgian Delphine Nkansa (11.06) completed the podium.

Like Hunt, Asher-Smith will have further opportunities to draw level with Croatian discus thrower Sandra Elkasevic and Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who earlier won a superb 5,000m gold on his comeback from injury.

Both will return to action on Wednesday, when attention turns to the women's 200m medals before the weekend's relays.

title: Who could Arsenal sign after missing out on Vinicius Jr?
description: One big signing missed, but one big signing through the doors - it's been a mixed transfer window for Arsenal.
fullText:
One big signing missed and one through the doors - it's been a mixed transfer window for Arsenal.

The Gunners were unsuccessful in what turned out to be a very public pursuit of Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr but did manage to bring in fellow Brazilian and Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes for £75m.

The signing of Guimaraes is another of the "win now" signings like Martin Zubimendi and Viktor Gyokeres last summer as he immediately raises the level and competition of the Arsenal squad.

Manager Mikel Arteta was asked if Arsenal supporters can expect more faces through the door before the deadline and the Spanish manager said: "Well, that's what we're trying to do. If we have the right player in the market to make us much better."

The Gunners are also going to be without two key defenders through injury in Jurrien Timber and William Saliba going into the start of this season, so it could be a busy few weeks in north London as they get set to try to defend their title.

Why Arsenal are signing Newcastle captain Guimaraes

Vinicius Jr and Real Madrid agree new six-year deal

For Arsenal it is hard to find any winger who would bring the excitement levels as well as the elite numbers that Vinicius Jr can.

So what other options do the club and sporting director Andrea Berta have?

Arsenal have come into this window looking at bringing in one or two forwards and Arteta has made it clearthat any player that comes in this season has to take the club to the next level.

Arsenal signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge to replace the outgoing Leandro Trossard, with the 24-year-old producing a remarkable 22 goals and 29 assists in all competitions last season for the Belgian club.

Replicating those numbers is unlikely but the Greek international has looked one of the brightest players during pre-season.

Arsenal have explored a move for Paris St-Germain winger Bradley Barcola, but Liverpool are also interested and the French side are demanding a fee of more than £100m for the forward.

Morgan Rogers, before he completed his move to Chelsea from Aston Villa for £117m, was a target but Arsenal were not willing to go above £80m for the England international.

Finding value in the market is hard and Berta is always looking to ensure that a deal represents value for the club.

Kenan Yildiz is one player from Europe who is on Arsenal's list in a hunt for a left winger.

The 21-year-old had a seriously impressive 2025-26 season for Juventus, scoring 11 goals and registering 10 assists in 47 appearances in all competitions.

The Turkey international can play across the frontline too which adds another dynamic, which may make him appealing to Arteta.

Like all good wingers he is unpredictable and can go on either the inside or outside, which means it is hard for defenders to know if he is going to cross the ball or shoot.

And stats from Opta show that, of all players in Europe's top five leagues last season, only Manchester United's Bruno Fernandes (98) and Werder Bremen's Romano Schmid (77) created more open-play chances than Yildiz, while it was only Vinicius (43) who created more chances after carrying the ball than Yildiz too (37).

However, Yildiz has just signed a new four-year deal and sources indicate that Juventus are unwilling to sell him.

Atletico Bilbao winger Nico Williams is another who has been looked at before by Arsenal and would add some spark to an attack which can be criticised as being too predictable at times.

The Spain winger has a contract until 2035 with the Basque club but there are reports which suggest there is a release clause in his contract.

Williams completed 43.8% of his 153 dribbles last season, scored six goals and registered three assists in a campaign that was disrupted by injury.

According to Opta, Williams averaged 8.2 dribbles per 90 minutes last season in La Liga with only Lamine Yamal, Kevin and Jeremy Doku averaging 

Availability is a big thing for Arteta and with a potentially high price tag and after a season of broken game time, this may not be the player for the Gunners at this point.

Arsenal also have the option of continuing with Tzolis on the left while they also have Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke who can fill that role too, with Eze playing from the left in some of Arsenal's biggest games at the business end of last season.

Guimaraes can ignite something different in us - Arteta

Arsenal are going to start the season with half of their first-choice back four out injured which means that any defender they sign is going to be required to play straight away.

That is why the Gunners have been interested in a move for Aston Villa defender Ezri Konsa who, as well as being a reliable centre-back, can play at right-back too.

Konsa has become a starting option for England and, alongside his importance to Villa, that will be why he is valued at around £60m.

However, Konsa is not the only defender that Arsenal have on their shortlist of targets.

The Gunners are interested in a move for Cristian Romero who is the captain of their rivals Tottenham Hotspur.

If any move does materialise for Romero, it would be a sensational development and be another deal, following the one for Eze last season, which would present a chance for bragging rights for Arsenal fans.

Atletico Madrid are reported to be chasing Romero though and with Spurs unlikely to want to strengthen their rivals, this deal seems unlikely to come to fruition.

One of the big moves of last season's summer transfer window was when Arsenal signed Gyokeres.

The Sweden striker was chosen to get the Gunners over the line in their hunt for a piece of silverware.

Gyokeres achieved that and scored 21 goals in all competitions but it was not always smooth sailing for the 28-year-old.

There are questions over his technical ability and about how suited he is to this Arsenal attack.

Arsenal have held a strong interest in Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez for sometime and the Argentinian international wants to leave the LaLiga club.

Alvarez, who was already played in the Premier League for Manchester City, would present a huge jump in quality and there would be no debate that he would make the Arsenal frontline better.

But, like many of the targets Arsenal are looking, at there is interest in Alvarez from elsewhere.

Barcelona are pursuing the forward which could scupper any plans that Arsenal have.

The Gunners are also trying to balance the books with Gabriel Jesus, Gabriel Martinelli and Reiss Nelson all available for a move if there is an offer that matches the club's value.

Denmark midfielder Christian Norgaard has already departed for Everton while there is not yet a clear path for academy graduate Ethan Nwaneri.

Arsenal have added Guimaraes and Tzolis as well as former Leeds goalkeeper Illan Meslier as back-up as they look to build on their success of last season.

But whatever happens, it is going to be a busy period in north London as they look to get their business finalised before the deadline.

title: The US Army is going digital, but soldiers still want physical backups of their battlefield maps
description: As the US Army undergoes a massive digital transformation, some soldiers are keeping their old physical copies in case the connection drops.
fullText:
US Army soldiers are testing a wave of new digital tools and weapons.

Some troops still rely on analog backups in case digital systems lose connection.

How much soldiers trust the new technology can come down to comfort level.

The US Army is embracing a massive digital transformation across systems and technologies, but that doesn't mean soldiers are ready to give up their physical, analog backups any time soon.

At a recent experimentation exercise at Fort Irwin in California, soldiers tested new digital maps and communications systems that Army leaders described as a major jump forward in streamlining decision-making. But troops said they still wanted physical counterparts for redundancy, ensuring they had fallback plans if network connections were lost.

The exercise, called Project Convergence Capstone, tested nearly 100 new technologies, including aerial and ground drones, electronic warfare capabilities, and the Army's prototype Next Generation Command and Control system, or NGC2, itself made up of a host of experimental pieces of hardware and software.

Some of the newest systems that Business Insider saw in action included NGC2's digital map application, which allows soldiers to see the locations of friendly forces and weapons in near real time. During an urban assault scenario, a soldier was seen using the map feature on his End User Device, a Samsung phone loaded with NGC2 software and worn in a carrier on the chest.

"Now I have good situational awareness of all of my elements around the battlefield in real time," Capt. Mohamed Elmaola with the 4th Infantry Division told Business Insider. "Digital enables me to get real-time, precise targeting feedback, which has been critical" to the fight.

That doesn't mean Elmaola is giving up his physical map, which he carried and updated while other soldiers flew a Black Widow quadcopter to assess enemy positions. The hard copy actually had some benefits that the digital version didn't.

"My analog copy is what I fight and live off because this gives me the totality of the story of what the enemy is doing, especially in a degraded environment," Elmaola said.

The degradation of the electromagnetic spectrum during the exercise, due to jamming and other electronic warfare effects, reinforced why Elmaola and others kept their physical maps close. If their EUDs or other digital assets went down, they'd need the analog versions to continue the fight.

The redundancy, Elmaola said, was crucial.

"This should never go away," he added, pointing to his physical map.

Other soldiers said physical maps were familiar from training. They would use the digital map to compare against and update their analog copies, while also using it to understand the overall battlefield situation.

Some Army leaders described the use of new technology, whether on its own or alongside analog copies, as coming down to individual preference.

"I find that the way we all interact with technology is a little bit different, and we all have different preferences," Maj. Gen. Patrick Ellis, commander of the 4th Infantry Division, said, adding that some use cases also likely came down to how comfortable soldiers were relying on technology.

Connectivity issues and the need for redundancy were major themes across the exercise, as the Army tested new digital technologies against electronic warfare and soldiers continued to fight when those systems weren't working. Some soldiers said systems like NGC2 could still work in limited capacities while under jamming, while others said connectivity problems had completely cut off their access.

Army leaders and soldiers said feedback from the exercise, particularly on how systems performed and what soldiers found most useful, was key to moving forward. The review process will focus on key questions around what systems were intended to do and whether they met those goals.

"It is probably the most critical thing that we're doing here, is taking observations and answering questions that we came in here to answer," Brig. Gen. Daniel Hibner, head of the Army Joint Modernization Command, said.

title: Trump signs executive order aimed at reducing number of recommended childhood vaccines
description: President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday aimed at reshaping the federal government’s approach toward childhood vaccines, insisting that infants should receive fewer immunizations ove...
fullText:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday aimed at reshaping the federal government's approach toward childhood vaccines, insisting that infants should receive fewer immunizations over a longer period despite little scientific evidence supporting such sweeping changes.

The wide-ranging order proposes reducing the total number of immunizations recommended for children in their earliest years and dividing the nation's childhood vaccine schedule into three categories.

It also advises that the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) vaccine be separated into three individual shots — a dramatic change that goes against broad scientific consensus but is in keeping with Trump's insistence in recent months that the widely administered shot be altered.

The administration signaled that it will push states to rework their vaccine requirements to incorporate the new federal guidelines, effectively upending longstanding practices aimed at improving childhood immunization rates.

"We're reducing them," Trump said from the Oval Office. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."

Flanked by an array of top health officials, including US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump made a range of misleading and incorrect claims about vaccines, including suggesting at one point that the MMR shot can be "quite lethal."

He alleged repeatedly and without evidence that children were being injected with more vaccines than they could handle, arguing that the shots should be spaced further apart. Pressed on his reasoning for recommending that infants receive their shots over five separate doctor visits, Trump said he'd done it with his children and "had no problem."

"Nothing bad can happen from what we're doing," he said of changes that health experts have long warned will reduce immunization rates and leave children more susceptible to disease. "Nothing bad can happen."

GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy, a doctor who expressed hesitancy last year over confirming Kennedy to the HHS post due to his positions on vaccines and autism, immediately criticized the order.

"This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism," Cassidy wrote on X. "Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe."

Under the order, the administration's new policy states that all children are recommended to receive vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Hib, pneumococcal disease, HPV and varicella, or chicken pox.

Only high-risk populations are now advised to receive respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) monoclonal antibodies and vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B, meningococcal B, meningococcal ACWY and dengue. That marks a change from the current schedule, which recommends that all children receive most of those shots.

Several of those, such as the hepatitis immunizations, would be based on what's called shared decision-making, or conversations with a healthcare provider. Those also include shots for rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and Covid-19.

The administration's new guidance suggests that that the immunizations be given over several medical visits "to give parents more options regarding the timing and frequency" of administration. But Trump offered a far blunter explanation from the Oval Office: He didn't believe that the current regimen was safe.

"Very simply: Large amounts of vaccine, large amounts of — like vats — of vaccine are currently pumped into your child's body," Trump said, at another point comparing the amount of vaccine given to children as "the size of a bottle of soda."

"We're doing 20% of that at each visit, and we'll let time elapse between visits so the body can handle this massive amount of fluid being pumped in," he said.

There is no evidence to support Trump's claims.

Trump's announcement hews closely to an HHS effort in January to whittle down the number of recommended vaccines in the childhood schedule. Medical groups sued to challenge that revised schedule, and a judge ruled in their favor, writing in his opinion that there are "glaring gaps" in expertise among the people Kennedy named to an independent advisory panel on vaccines last year.

Referencing that earlier effort, White House adviser Heidi Overton said Monday that administration officials "are going to be working directly with states so that we're not reliant on the court case to resolve. We are doing it right away so that parents get the benefit from state laws changing."

The vaccine announcement came shortly after Senate Republicans released 2021 text messages obtained from Dr. Anthony Fauci's government phone showing the former top health official discussing possible risks of the Covid-19 vaccine to pregnant women. Later studies showed that the vaccines were safe during pregnancy.

Asked about a push by Republican senators for the Justice Department to charge Fauci with contempt of Congress, Trump said he'd yet to talk about it with US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro.

The Monday order on vaccines followed months of escalating pressure that Trump had put on Kennedy for more action on the childhood vaccine schedule, as the two men both publicly speculate about links between vaccines and autism.

There have been extensive scientific studies of vaccines that have yielded no evidence of a connection to autism.

It also came despite long-running reservations among Trump's political advisers that advancing controversial vaccine policies is widely unpopular and could alienate voters ahead of November's midterms.

White House officials earlier this year urged Kennedy to shift his focus to other, more mainstream initiatives due to concerns about the political fallout, though his department's work on vaccines has continued in the background.

"This is something very important for all of us," Trump said. "Very happy to sign it."

Yet questions swirled Monday about the mechanics of separating out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines, particularly because those are not sold separately in the US market.

HHS is working with the private sector to make those commercially available, and Kennedy is expected to produce a plan for separate vaccines within 90 days, a White House official said Monday.

"The president has long held that the MMR vaccine should be separated and wants that available as an option," the official said.

Another White House official said, "This isn't just the president …arbitrarily setting vaccine policy." The official pointed to a January scientific assessment that HHS carried out before unveiling the proposed schedule that was eventually blocked in court.

That assessment does not specifically address the utility, safety or effectiveness of separating the measles, mumps and rubella shots.

Concerns spiked Monday among pediatricians and medical groups that removing broad recommendations for certain childhood vaccines could mean out-of-pocket costs for parents who do want to fully vaccinate their children.

The new contingent on the panel, some of whom have stated objections to vaccines, has already discussed delaying hepatitis B vaccination from infancy to 12 years of age. The changes ordered by Trump on Monday would recommend hepatitis immunizations only for high-risk populations.

"They still are a recommendation, and so we assume that that means they'll still be covered by insurance and fully available to parents that want them," the first official said Monday.

This story has been updated with additional reporting and developments.

title: A DC trial was nearing its end when the jury made a discovery that shocked everyone in the courtroom
description: The charges at a month-long criminal trial in Washington’s federal court last month were fairly straightforward: That one man had allegedly held up seven 7-Elevens and a few other gas stations in spri...
fullText:
The charges at a monthlong criminal trial in Washington's federal court last month were fairly straightforward: That one man had allegedly held up seven 7-Elevens and a few other gas stations in spring 2023 and stolen cars.

But the trial of Shamell Naquan Joyner had a twist. While deliberating, jurors found a Chinese yuan in one sweatshirt that was in evidence. And inside a jacket that was also part of the case, they found suspicious white powder in a folded up piece of paper. The prosecutors and judge said it appeared to be drugs.

The DC US Attorney's Office, law enforcement on the case and the defense team hadn't known.

The events of the jury deliberation raised eyebrows across the federal court in recent days, as word spread of what happened.

During deliberations, jurors are allowed to review evidence that is presented during the trial. Had the suspected drugs and yuan been part of the prosecution's case ahead of trial, it could have supported the case. But because it was a surprise, it could have been considered unfair to Joyner.

Several longtime lawyers in Washington told CNN last week they hadn't heard of a situation as embarrassing as this one, though some former prosecutors in DC conceded that every few years, a jury might land upon a piece of evidence that wasn't examined by law enforcement thoroughly enough.

Judge Rudolph Contreras, who presided over the trial, was flabbergasted.

"The Court shares Mr. Joyner's amazement at law enforcement's failure to uncover the Chinese Yuan, note, and powdery substance in the physical evidence," the judge, who has a decade of experience on the bench, wrote in an opinion a few days later.

"Mr. Liolos, who I know is from New York, is probably astonished that any money got past the police department," the judge also said on the bench, referring to John Liolos, one of Joyner's lawyers.

The FBI declined to comment when asked how agents on the case weren't aware of the drugs and money in the pockets.

When asked about how the evidence oversight happened, a spokesperson for the DC US Attorney's Office didn't answer directly.

Prosecutors alleged Joyner had robbed 10 convenience stores and gas stations in central Washington, Maryland and northern Virginia in the spring of 2023. The robberies at first started a few days apart in April, then by May 2, Joyner was hitting several in the same day, they alleged. He also was accused of armed carjackings around two of the days that the armed robberies occurred.

The series of incidents resulted in a 28-count indictment against Joyner in 2023. He wasn't charged with drug possession.

The case was big for the US Attorney's Office. The trial lasted a full month, with the jury hearing witnesses testify over 10 trial days, then deliberations lasting another week. Joyner had as many as nine lawyers and three prosecutors at trial.

As the jury was leaving on July 22, their second day of deliberations, a juror told courthouse staff they had found some items inside a jacket and a sweatshirt found in one of the carjacked cars that had been worn by the alleged robber.

"We were looking at (the jacket), and (one of the jurors) reached in the breast pocket and she pulled out — it looked like a receipt, but there was a white powder or white substance inside," the jury foreperson told the court on July 23, the next morning, according to a trial transcript obtained by CNN.

"Some of it, kind of, spilled out a little bit, but (a juror) put it back in the pocket and we put it back in the bag," the unnamed juror said.

There was a sweatshirt the jurors could examine too as evidence in the jury room. A juror had looked in the pocket there "and he pulled out — it was crumpled up — it was a bill … one of the Chinese Yuan bills," the foreperson then said.

When the jurors found the suspected drugs and money in the pockets at the end of the second day of jury deliberations, the issue opened up major legal questions for Joyner.

Both items of clothing had been key evidence putting Joyner at the scene of two of the May 2 robberies, and were inside the Toyota he was accused of stealing when police captured it a few days later.

Would the jurors be prejudiced against Joyner now? Had the jury finding the suspected drugs corroborated witness testimony from the trial further than what Joyner's defense lawyers anticipated?

The Justice Department argued that a witness testified about Joyner stealing money during the armed robbery of four different convenience stores. At one of the 7-Elevens, a witness said the robber took his wallet, and it had in it a Chinese Yuan from a college study abroad trip.

A cooperator who drove Joyner separately testified Joyner had paid him in drugs the night Joyner allegedly held up a gas station. The jacket with the apparent drugs in the pocket had been worn by the armed robber.

After the discovery in the pockets, Contreras brought each of the jurors into the courtroom one by one.

He told them the Chinese bill and the apparent drugs weren't part of the evidence in the case. The jurors each told the court they could set aside those items in their consideration of the case against Joyner.

They went back to deliberating.

The following Monday — the fifth day of deliberations — the jury had reached another predicament.

They said they realized they couldn't agree on more than half of the charges — representing five of the alleged armed robberies and one carjacking — Joyner faced.

"The jury remains deadlocked on or unable to vote on the remaining 15 counts in this case," they said in a note to the judge. "Our differences are in the areas of what constitutes a reasonable doubt and in how to determine identity beyond a reasonable doubt … In the absence of additional evidence or testimony, we cannot reach verdicts on the remaining 15 counts."

So, Contreras ended deliberations, taking a partial verdict.

The diligence of the jury, unable to come to an agreement on several of the charges against Joyner, echoed an unusual challenge the US Attorney's Office has faced in several other criminal trials this year.

Still, the jury found Joyner guilty of 13 criminal charges, representing an armed robbery in mid-April 2023 in downtown Washington, and four armed robberies and a carjacking on May 2, 2023, in Northwest Washington and Maryland.

"The jury's verdict ensures the defendant will face a 31year mandatory minimum sentence, making the D.C. community safer with this serial robber off the streets," a spokesperson from the US Attorney's Office said about the case.

Joyner's defense attorneys haven't yet appealed his conviction. They declined to comment because a final judgment in the case is not set in stone.

Correction: This story was updated to correct the year Joyner was indicted, which was 2023.

title: Storms from Dolphin soak China's east, ground nearly 950 Shanghai flights
description: Torrential rain and storms in Typhoon Dolphin's wake inundated several provinces in China's east, drenching the coastal region and
fullText:
SHANGHAI/BEIJING, Aug 10 (Reuters) - Torrential rain and storms in Typhoon Dolphin's wake inundated several provinces in China's east, drenching the coastal region and flooding streets in Shanghai, where around 40% of flights were grounded on Monday due to the weather.

Dolphin packed maximum sustained ‌winds of 151 kph near its centre when it made landfall in Zhejiang, the province to the south and west of Shanghai, on Sunday ‌evening before weakening to a tropical storm.

Its remaining rain clouds continued to soak the eastern provinces including Anhui, Jiangsu and Shandong on Monday.

Many streets in Shanghai, the country's second most populous city, were flooded, including in ​the main commercial centres.

The city's two airports cancelled a total of 943 flights due to the typhoon, reducing capacity by nearly 40%, state broadcaster CCTV said.

China Eastern Airlines said on Monday it was trying to resume flights to Shanghai, Zhejiang and other destinations in an "orderly manner."

Many streets in Shanghai's suburban Jiading and Qingpu districts around the city centre remained waterlogged, according to live-streams shared by residents on social media. The live videos, not verified by Reuters, showed people wading through knee-high murky water.

"It rained almost all night last night. ‌When I woke up this morning, I found the neighbourhood ⁠flooded, and the streets were severely flooded," said 39-year-old Hou Lina, who works in sales in Jiading in Shanghai.

"I've lived in Shanghai for 10 years, and this is the first time I've experienced such inconvenience from a typhoon. This is the first time ⁠I've encountered such widespread flooding," she told Reuters.

In Shanghai's Jinshan, the district authority said non-essential businesses and organisations could temporarily halt operations, classes, outdoor events and transit services, amid forecasts of continued strong winds and heavy rain on Monday.

Powerful winds and lashing rain flipped over a truck in Zhejiang's Wenzhou, a video posted on TikTok on Sunday showed. It was not clear ​what ​happened to the driver.

Authorities warned that 74 rivers in the Taihu Lake basin and the coastal areas ​of eastern Zhejiang have exceeded warning levels, and that flood risks ‌for small and medium-sized rivers in heavy rainfall areas are high.

RAIN AND FLOOD WARNINGS FOR BEIJING, HEAT FOR HONG KONG

The strongest typhoon to hit China this year, Dolphin is forecast to move deeper inland to the central provinces of Hubei and Henan in the coming days while also pushing moisture north.

Authorities in the capital Beijing raised warnings for torrential rain and said the city was prepared to activate its flood control response on Tuesday morning.

Beijing is expected to experience "significant rainfall" from Tuesday until Thursday, with authorities warning of the risk of flash floods in the city and landslides in the surrounding mountainous areas.

The typhoon had already travelled 6,000 km (3,728 miles) before it made ‌landfall, giving it a life-cycle three times longer than an ordinary typhoon, and bringing with it ​an ultra-large cloud system that enveloped China's east, CCTV said in another report.

Dolphin's impact was also being ​compared to Doksuri in 2023. That typhoon crossed the country after causing ​destruction in southeastern Fujian province, unleashing record-breaking rainfall in Beijing.

As the storm clouds meet colder air in the north, Beijing, Tianjin and ‌Hebei will need to brace for heavy rain into Thursday, CCTV ​said.

Hong Kong, on China's southern coast, has seen ​extreme heat due to Dolphin, recording its hottest day ever on Sunday at 36.9 degrees Celsius, the highest since records began in 1884, according to the Hong Kong Observatory, the territory's weather body.

TSR (Tropical Storm Risk) said it expected the 2026 northwest Pacific typhoon season to be one of the most active ​on record and to include 28 tropical storms, 20 typhoons ‌and 13 intense typhoons.

TSR said the ongoing strong El Niño event, high activity to date and weaker-than-normal trade winds across the northwest Pacific ​basin, were key reasons for the intensity of the typhoon season.

title: Joe Scarborough goes scorched earth on Democrats not separating themselves from Hasan Piker
description: Joe Scarborough blasts Democrats as "too woke" to condemn Hasan Piker's rhetoric after ally Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Senate primary race.
fullText:
MS NOW "Morning Joe" host Joe Scarborough launched a blistering attack on far-left streamer Hasan Piker and Democrats unwilling to distance themselves from his rhetoric Monday, warning the party risked repeating what he viewed as its costly 2024 mistakes after Piker ally Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Democratic Senate nomination.

Scarborough, raising his voice and shouting at times, said Democrats were "too woke to call out the obvious" and questioned why party leaders were reluctant to draw a line over Piker's past comments about rape during Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack, when he remarked that it didn't matter to him if it occurred.

"This is about the Democrats once again, fumbling the football on the two-yard line when they have a chance to make great gains, but being so woke, I don't know if you want to call it woke 1, woke 2, or woke 3, but being too woke to call out the obvious!" Scarborough yelled. "I swear to God. It's really, it's crazy that we're even having this conversation."

The Republican National Committee (RNC) has sought to turn El-Sayed's continued relationship with Piker into a general election liability. RNC national spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Fox News Digital Sunday that Democrats' unwillingness to disavow the streamer reflected a broader problem for the party.

Mark Halperin Calls Hasan Piker A 'Horrible Person' As Democrats Face Pressure To Distance From Streamer

"El-Sayed is a terrorist sympathizer and an America-hating socialist. His refusal to distance himself from Hamas-hugging radicals like Hasan Piker reaffirms his true allegiance is to terrorist groups, not America. Democrats' refusal to disavow this clown shows they either share his poisonous ideology or they're too cowardly to confront it," Baldassarre said.

"The Democrat Party is being driven off [a] cliff by socialists who are driving blindfolded while arguing about the view. Unless Democrats hit the brakes, every candidate on the ballot will have to answer for socialists' outrageous beliefs that will bankrupt our country and strip every American of safety, sanity, and freedom," she added.

Scarborough specifically called on Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., to demand that candidates distance themselves from such rhetoric.

"If somebody says, a woman being raped doesn't matter in the grand scheme of things, it's OK to call that person out and demand that candidates distance themselves from those people!" Scarborough shouted.

Fetterman 'Dares' El-sayed To Stick With Piker, Claims Michigan Nominee Has 'Little Man Syndrome Energy'

The fight has intensified since El-Sayed narrowly defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers for the seat held by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

Piker made repeated appearances with El-Sayed, including at a Detroit pool party the night before the primary. El-Sayed has rejected Piker's most controversial remarks but resisted calls to sever ties.

"Of course I oppose rape. Of course I don't think 9/11 was justified," El-Sayed said during an April appearance on "Fox & Friends." "[Just] because you appear with somebody, doesn't mean you agree with them on everything."

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., has also challenged El-Sayed to maintain the relationship now that he must appeal beyond Democratic primary voters.

Johnson Turns Democrats' Socialist Civil War Into New Weapon For Midterms

"I dare you to continue to campaign with people like Hasan Piker because he now will quickly find out it's easy to campaign in the echo chamber as a Democrat," Fetterman told Fox News Digital.

Piker has pushed Democrats in the opposite direction, calling for party members who refuse to support El-Sayed to be "punished," while centrist Democratic group Third Way recently announced a $15 million campaign aimed at weakening the Democratic Socialists of America's influence.

Scarborough said the debate reminded him of Democrats' failure to recognize cultural issues that hurt them during the 2024 election.

"Why are we bringing this up now? We're bringing this up now because it seems an awful lot like what was happening in 2024 when Democrats couldn't get out of their own way to win an election they should have won," he said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DNC, El-Sayed, Piker and Schumer for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

title: Democratic Michigan AG accuses her party of 'absolutely not' doing enough to counter antisemitism
description: Michigan AG Dana Nessel told MS NOW that five Democrats charged with antisemitic acts are still permitted to attend the Michigan Democratic Party convention.
fullText:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel accused the Michigan Democratic Party on Monday of not doing enough to address antisemitism by allowing members charged with antisemitic acts to still attend the upcoming convention.

Nessel previously told Jewish leaders and community members that she would not attend the convention scheduled for Aug. 29 out of security concerns. As the state's first Jewish attorney general, Nessel told MS NOW that she was familiar with antisemitism while in office, but the Democratic Party has now become intolerant of different ideas.

"Look, myself and other Jewish electeds are subjected to a barrage of antisemitic threats," Nessel said. "And that's been happening literally since my first day in office in 2019, long before Oct. 7. But in addition to that, you know, what we've seen in the Democratic Party as of late in here in Michigan is that we're not seeing the same kind of civil discourse that we used to be able to have and the ability to have a diversity of ideas and opinions that are, you know, respected."

Left-wing Activists Heckle Pro-israel Democrat Haley Stevens At Michigan Convention

When asked whether the party was doing enough to counter antisemitism, Nessel replied "absolutely not" and claimed that criminally charged Democrats were still allowed to attend the convention.

"We have five members of the Democratic Party who have been charged with antisemitic acts of vandalism and harassment and threats to other Democratic officials, some of whom are Jewish and including an attack on the Jewish Federation of Detroit," Nessel said. "So those people are still permitted to come to the convention. And it's just baffling to me that while these charges are pending, they're going to be allowed to be there despite, you know, these credible charges against them."

She added, "So I think that there's a lot that we could do. We could enforce a code of conduct that says that, again, you can't chase people around the convention yelling at them. It's not appropriate to boo people off the stage even if it's a candidate whose ideas you don't support."

Jewish Michigan Democrats Admit They Will Vote Republican If Abdul El-sayed Becomes Nominee

In a comment to Fox News Digital, Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said, "We are appalled by the details of this indictment and the hateful, antisemitic threats that took place. The Michigan Democratic Party condemns all acts of hatred and violence, which have no place in Michigan and should not be tolerated."

Another Michigan Democratic Party spokesperson said that the party received a code of conduct complaint but will not comment on pending investigations.

"We are committed to ensuring party-hosted events are safe and secure environments for all attendees. We reject antisemitism, Islamophobia, and all forms of hateful conduct. We are working diligently with stakeholders, elected officials, and party membership to prepare for our August convention and look forward to welcoming Michigan Democrats to the Lansing Center on Aug. 29," the spokesperson said.

Fetterman 'Dares' El-sayed To Stick With Piker, Claims Michigan Nominee Has 'Little Man Syndrome Energy'

During the interview, Nessel also addressed Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, whose campaign has been embroiled in antisemitic controversies based on his past comments. Though she did not explicitly endorse El-Sayed, Nessel told MS NOW that she has no desire to see GOP candidate Mike Rogers win the Senate seat and that she plans on speaking with El-Sayed about her concerns soon.

"First of all, I'd like him to tone down his rhetoric a little bit," Nessel said. "And what I mean by that is, AIPAC — which many of us do not support or agree with — and Israel, with many of us who do not support or agree with their government or the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu, they cannot be the central villain in literally every story."

She continued, "If we're talking about reforming healthcare, which all of us want to do in the party, it's not AIPAC that is responsible for those problems, it's the health insurance and pharmaceutical companies," adding, "Not everything is about AIPAC, not everything is about Israel."

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

title: Authorities ID the officer who fatally shot a Black man on a bike in Madison, Wisconsin
description: Investigators on Monday released the name of the Madison police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in July — a shooting that was captured on video and sparked protests that put Wiscon...
fullText:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Investigators on Monday released the name of the Madison police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in July — a shooting that was captured on video and sparked protests that put Wisconsin's capital city on edge over how authorities treat people of color.

Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, a white officer with nearly 11 years' experience in law enforcement, fired the shots that killed Corey Ruiz on July 22, the Wisconsin Department of Justice's Division of Criminal Investigation said in a statement. Baitinger-Peterson was one of four officers who surrounded Ruiz, who was on a bike, in response to calls about someone who was checking out parked cars and an alleged burglary attempt, police said.

The shooting sparked days of protests and calls from the Black community for Madison to address racial justice issues.

Baitinger-Peterson did not reply to an email seeking comment.

Jim Palmer, executive director of the Wisconsin Professional Police Association, which is the state's largest police union and represents Madison officers, responded on behalf of Baitinger-Peterson.

"I am deeply concerned for the safety and privacy of him, his family, and the other officers involved," Palmer said.

He said those concerns are being taken seriously and "appropriate precautions" are in place.

"I urge everyone to allow the investigation to proceed and to refrain from prejudging the officers or placing them and their families at further risk," Palmer said.

Baitinger-Peterson and the other three officers who interacted with Ruiz that day have been placed on paid administrative leave while the state investigates the shooting.

There is no timeline for when the state Justice Department investigation will conclude. Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne will review the findings before deciding whether to file charges against Baitinger-Peterson.

Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents Ruiz's family, has called for the officer to be charged.

While bystanders captured the confrontation on video, there is no body camera footage because Madison police officers don't wear them.

The state Justice Department said two officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz but weren't successful. Ruiz "brandished a knife and injured" Baitinger-Peterson, it said. Law enforcement agencies haven't divulged the extent of the officer's injuries. They did release an image of a fixed-blade knife that was recovered at the scene.

The protests over the shooting led to several nearby community events being canceled or postponed.
